story.title: Sam and the Glow-Green Gecko
story.subtitle: A sticky, silly climb through the animal kingdom.

chapters.heading: Chapter One: The Gecko Wakes Up
chapters.text:
Sam was supposed to be asleep.

Instead, he lay on his bedroom floor, counting spider legs on his poster. Eight legs, every single spider. Sam loved spiders. He loved geckos too. He picked up every bug in the backyard, even the wiggly ones.

On his shelf sat his favorite toy, a little green gecko named Gordo. Tonight, Gordo's eyes went GLOW.

Sam sat up fast. 'Gordo?'

Gordo blinked. He skittered sideways, right up the wall. He did not fall. He hung there, upside down, grinning.

'Wanna know my secret?' Gordo asked.

Sam nodded so hard his hair flopped. 'Climb on,' said Gordo. 'We're going wall-hunting tonight.'

Sam grabbed his bug magnifier from the windowsill. He held it up to Gordo's foot. 'Whoa,' Sam whispered. 'Your toes have squiggles!'

'Those squiggles are **tiny hairs**,' said Gordo. 'So many, you could never count them. Millions and millions! They are so small, your eyes alone cannot see them. That's my secret. The hairs hug the wall, holding on tight, like a million tiny hugs.'

Sam pressed his own hand flat on the wall, then let go. His hand slid right off. 'No hairs on me,' Sam said.

'Nope,' laughed Gordo. 'Just you and me, buddy. Hop on my back.'

**WHOOOOSH!** Sam shrank down, down, down, until he was gecko-sized, riding on Gordo's back.

They scampered up the wall together. Sam felt Gordo's foot peel off the glass, toe by toe, easy as pulling up tape. 'It's not glue,' Sam said, surprised. 'You just let go.'

'Good eye!' said Gordo. 'No mess, no glue, no sticky goo left behind. Just peel and go.'

Gordo wiggled his eyebrows. 'Not bad for toe number one. Eleven more world-famous toes to go.'

'TOES ROCK!' Sam shouted.

chapters.heading: Chapter Two: Sam's Favorite Spider
chapters.text:
**CLICK.** Gordo's claws tapped the glass window. Something else was already there.

A spider sat on the window, eight legs spread wide. Sam gasped. 'A spider! My favorite!'

The spider walked straight up the glass, calm as can be. Sam tilted his head. 'Does it have hairs too? Like you?'

Gordo grinned. 'Smart guess. Look close.'

Sam pressed his magnifier to the glass. Tiny hairs covered every spider leg, thousands of them, like fuzzy little brushes.

'Spiders have **tiny hairs** on their feet too,' said Gordo. 'Not the exact same as mine, but the same clever idea. That's how they climb smooth glass, just like me.'

Sam remembered something from the garden. 'I saw a spider climb our fence last week! I thought it was magic.'

'Not magic,' said Gordo. 'Just hairy feet and a whole lot of practice.'

The spider scuttled sideways, then stopped near Sam's hand. Sam did not grab it. He knew better. 'Hi, friend,' Sam whispered instead. 'I'm just looking.'

Gordo nudged him with a tiny elbow. 'Good job watching, not grabbing. Even the best bug-catcher knows when to just say hello.'

Gordo tapped Sam's nose. 'Big fan club for the eight-legged crew.' Sam laughed so hard he nearly slid off Gordo's back, but Gordo held tight. No slipping. No sliding.

The spider waved a leg, then climbed off into the night. Sam waved back.

chapters.heading: Chapter Three: Sticky Drops and Switching Tools
chapters.text:
**BZZZZ.** A fly landed on the window, right next to where the spider had been.

Sam watched it walk upside down on the glass, easy as walking on the floor. 'How does the fly do it? It doesn't look hairy.'

Gordo peeked through the magnifier. 'Look at its feet. See those tiny shiny dots?'

Sam looked hard. Tiny drops glistened under each fly foot. 'It's wet!'

'Flies ooze little sticky drops from their feet,' said Gordo. 'Like tiny dabs of glue, made by their own body. Sticky enough to hold, easy enough to walk.'

Just then, an ant marched up the brick outside, and a cockroach scurried along right behind it. Sam pointed. 'Two more climbers!'

'Ants and cockroaches are extra clever,' said Gordo. 'On bumpy brick, they dig in with sharp little claws. On smooth glass, they switch to sticky pads instead. They pick the right tool for the wall.'

Sam clapped. 'Like how I use my net for butterflies and my jar for ladybugs!'

'Exactly like that,' said Gordo. 'Different job, different tool.'

Sam counted on his fingers. 'Gecko hairs. Spider hairs. Fly glue drops. Ant claws and pads. That's four tricks already!'

'Five, counting mine and yours,' Gordo winked. 'Oh wait, I only have one trick. You have zero.'

Sam giggled and swatted at him, gently, and Gordo swatted right back.

chapters.heading: Chapter Four: The Goat on the Cliff
chapters.text:
**WHOOOOSH!** The window became a mountain, steep and rocky.

A mountain goat stood on a cliff, way up high. Sam looked down. It was a long way down!

'Don't worry,' said Gordo quickly. 'Goats never slip. Watch.'

The goat hopped from rock to rock, sure-footed as can be. Sam watched its feet closely. 'Its feet look weird. Hard on the edge, squishy in the middle.'

'Good eye again!' said Gordo. 'A mountain goat's **hooves**, that means its hard feet, have a tough rim around the edge and a soft, squishy pad in the middle. The soft part molds right onto the bumpy rock.'

Sam tried wiggling his own toes inside his socks. 'My feet don't do that.'

'Nope,' Gordo laughed. 'But I bet you're a champion at climbing the couch.'

Sam puffed out his chest. He hopped from cushion to cushion, just like the goat hopped from rock to rock, until he landed safely on the rug.

'COUCH CHAMPION!' Sam yelled.

'See?' said Gordo. 'Everybody's got their own cliff.'

chapters.heading: Chapter Five: Squirrel Claws and Frog Toes
chapters.text:
**SCRITCH SCRATCH.** A squirrel zipped straight up a tree trunk outside.

Sam pressed his face to the window. 'How is it going so fast?'

'Claws,' said Gordo. 'Sharp, curved claws. They dig into tiny cracks and bumps, too small for us to even see.'

Sam squinted at the tree bark. 'I don't see any cracks.'

'That's the trick,' said Gordo. 'The squirrel doesn't need big cracks. Tiny ones are enough, if your claws are sharp enough.'

On a leaf below, something small and green sat very still. Sam spotted it first. 'A frog! On a leaf, upside down!'

Gordo looked closer. 'A tree frog. Check out its toes.'

Sam squished his nose to the glass. The frog's toes were flat, round, and a little slimy, with tiny patterns like honeycomb. 'Its toes are squishy and wet.'

'That squishy, wet stuff is a bit of slime,' said Gordo. 'It helps the frog's flat toe pads stick to wet, slippery leaves. Claws for the squirrel, slime for the frog. Different animal, different trick.'

Sam grinned. 'This is the best bedtime ever.'

'Every bedtime with me is,' said Gordo, not even a little bit modest.

chapters.heading: Chapter Six: The Slow, Slimy Snail
chapters.text:
**SQUELCH.** Something small and slow was climbing the garden wall.

A snail. Sam crouched down to watch it move. 'It's so slow!'

'Slow, but it never falls,' said Gordo. 'Look behind it.'

Sam saw a shiny, wet trail left on the brick. 'Ewww. Slimy!'

'That slime is the secret,' said Gordo. 'The snail glides along on its own slime. Its squishy foot grips and ripples, little wave after little wave, pushing it up the wall.'

Sam tried to make his own hand ripple like a wave. It just flopped around. 'I can't do it.'

Sam grabbed his sock and dragged it along the floor. 'Look, I made a trail too!'

'That's a sock trail,' Gordo laughed. 'Not quite the same as snail slime, but a solid try.'

Sam leaned close, careful not to touch. 'Hi, slow friend. Keep gliding.'

The snail did not answer. Snails never do. But it kept gliding, slow and steady, all the way to the top of the wall.

chapters.heading: Chapter Seven: Upside-Down Bat, Straight-Up Woodpecker
chapters.text:
**FLUTTER FLUTTER.** Something swooped by in the dark and landed on a branch.

A bat, hanging completely upside down. Sam laughed. 'Silly bat, you're upside down!'

'That's just how bats sleep,' said Gordo. 'They can't climb fast like me. But their feet have curved claws, strong enough to hang on all night without ever letting go.'

Sam hung upside down off his own bed later, just to try it. His face went red fast. 'Bats are tougher than me!'

**TAP TAP TAP.** A woodpecker landed on the tree trunk, climbing straight up.

Sam noticed something. 'Its tail is pushed against the tree. Like a little chair.'

'Smart spotting!' said Gordo. 'The woodpecker's stiff tail feathers prop it up, like a kickstand. And its toes grip two forward, two backward, for extra holding power.'

Sam tapped his own knuckles on the windowsill. TAP TAP TAP. 'I'm a woodpecker too!'

'Close,' Gordo grinned, 'but your tail isn't stiff enough yet.'

Sam tried standing with his feet turned funny, two toes pointing one way. He wobbled and giggled and flopped onto the rug.

'Not quite a woodpecker,' Gordo laughed, 'but an A-plus try.'

chapters.heading: Chapter Eight: The Climbing Paddle
chapters.text:
**WHOOOOSH!** The mountain, the tree, and the garden all faded. Sam's bedroom wall came back.

'One more stop,' said Gordo. 'This one's my favorite, because it's about people.'

A picture glowed on the wall: a person climbing straight up a glass wall, using two flat paddles.

'Whoa! A person climbing like a gecko!' Sam said.

'In **2014**, scientists built sticky paddles, copying gecko feet,' said Gordo. 'A person pressed them on glass and climbed right up, just like me, just bigger.'

Sam gasped. 'People can be geckos too!'

'With the right invention, sure,' said Gordo. 'Scientists studied my sticky toes so closely, they figured out how to copy the trick.'

Sam counted sleepily on his fingers. 'Gecko, spider, fly, ant, goat, squirrel, frog, snail, bat, woodpecker... and now people too.'

'Quite a list,' said Gordo. 'And you found every single trick yourself.'

Sam yawned, a huge, jaw-cracking yawn. 'Can we copy it? Tomorrow? With cardboard paddles?'

'Tomorrow,' Gordo promised. 'Tonight, bed.'

**WHOOOOSH!** Sam shrank back to his normal size, standing on his bedroom carpet. Gordo climbed down off the wall and settled back onto the shelf, eyes dimming to a soft glow.

Sam climbed into bed, one hand still holding his bug magnifier. On his nightstand sat a tiny paper paddle, folded from a sticky note, left right there from their climb.

'Night, Gordo,' Sam whispered.

'Stick with it, Sam,' Gordo whispered back, and his glow faded to sleep.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Sam. Stick with it.

true_facts.text: Gecko toes have **millions of tiny hairs** that help them climb glass and walk on ceilings.
Those hairs are so **tiny**, you cannot even see them without a special magnifier.
A gecko's grip isn't glue. It can **peel its toes off**, easy as pulling up tape.
Spiders have **tiny hairs** on their feet too, which is how they climb smooth glass.
Flies climb using **sticky drops** that ooze out of their feet, like tiny bits of glue.
Ants and cockroaches use **sharp claws** on bumpy walls and **sticky pads** on smooth ones.
A mountain goat's **hooves** have a hard edge and a soft, squishy middle that grips rocky cliffs.
Squirrels dig **sharp, curved claws** into tiny cracks too small for us to see.
Tree frogs have **flat, slimy toe pads** that help them stick to wet leaves.
Snails climb walls by gliding along on their own **slime**, in little rippling waves.
Bats hang upside down using **curved claws**, strong enough to hold on all night.
Woodpeckers climb straight up trees using a **stiff tail** for support and toes that grip two ways.
In **2014**, scientists made sticky paddles copied from gecko feet, so a person could climb a glass wall.

new_recurring.name: Gordo the Gecko
new_recurring.rule: A glow-eyed toy gecko on Sam's shelf who lights up at bedtime, shrinks or grows Sam to gecko-size, and guides him on real animal-fact adventures. His catchphrase is 'Stick with it!'

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Sam fell asleep holding his bug magnifier, with a tiny paper climbing paddle folded from a sticky note on his nightstand, while Gordo the toy gecko glowed softly back to sleep on the shelf.

story.title: Finn, Nell, and the Golden Honey Jar
story.subtitle: A buzzy bedtime adventure into the hive

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Golden Jar Glows
chapters.text:
Finn sat on the kitchen floor with a plate of honey toast. He licked the sticky gold off his fingers.

Nell lay on the rug nearby. She drew a big yellow flower with a yellow crayon.

The house was quiet. It was almost bedtime.

Then — HUMMMMM. A jar of honey on the counter began to glow. It glowed soft and gold, like a tiny sun.

Nell saw it first. "Finn! Look! The jar is glowing!"

Finn hopped up. He touched the lid. CLICK! A tiny door opened in the glass, no bigger than a thumbnail.

A little yellow bee zoomed out. She had stripy wings and a big smile.

"Hello! I'm Buzzby!" she said. "I'm a scout bee. I find good flowers. Want to see how bees make honey?"

Nell grinned. "Yes! I love yellow. And flowers!"

Finn nodded. "I love honey on toast!"

Buzzby waved a wing. "Then hold on, both of you. We're going to get small!"

The jar glowed brighter. WHOOOOSH! Finn and Nell felt tiny and light, like dandelion fluff. The kitchen grew huge around them.

Buzzby led them through the tiny door. Inside was a golden hallway that smelled like flowers and warm sugar.

"Where are we going?" Finn asked.

"To my hive," said Buzzby. "That's my bee house. It's buzzing full of my sisters."

Nell giggled. "Sisters? How many?"

"Lots," said Buzzby. "Let's go count them."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: So Many Sisters
chapters.text:
BUZZZZZZ! The sound got louder and louder. Then they landed at a huge, round hive. It looked like a stack of golden rooms.

Bees flew in and out, busy as can be.

"Whoa," said Finn. "How many bees live here?"

Buzzby smiled. "Guess!"

Finn thought hard. "Um... a hundred?"

"More!" said Buzzby. "In summer, a hive can have up to sixty thousand bees. That's so many, you could never count them all!"

Nell's eyes went wide. "Sixty thousand? That's more than all my toys!"

"Most of us are girls," Buzzby said. "We're called worker bees. We do every job. Flying, cleaning, making honey — everything!"

"Everything?" Nell asked.

"Almost everything," said Buzzby. "One bee doesn't work. She just lays eggs. Lots and lots of eggs."

"Who's that?" Finn asked.

"The queen," Buzzby said. "Follow me. You'll meet her."

They zoomed past rows of bees, all buzzing hello.

Nell waved at every single one. "Hi! Hi! Hi!"

By the time they reached the middle of the hive, her wing was tired from waving so much. Finn laughed.

"You can't say hi to sixty thousand bees, Nell!"

"I can try!" said Nell, and waved one more time.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Queen's Busy Day
chapters.text:
In the middle of the hive sat the biggest bee of all. She had a long, shiny body. Little bees fussed around her, bringing her food.

"That's the queen," Buzzby whispered.

Finn stepped closer. "Hi, Queen Bee! What's your job?"

The queen bee smiled. "I lay eggs. Lots of eggs. Sometimes more than a thousand in one single day!"

Nell gasped. "A thousand? In ONE day?"

"That's a whole hive's worth of new bees," said Buzzby.

Finn tilted his head. "Can we watch you lay one?"

"Of course," said the queen. She wiggled into a tiny six-sided hole. POP! A tiny white egg appeared inside.

"She does that again and again," Buzzby said. "All day long."

Nell counted the holes around them. "One, two, three... there's SO many holes!"

"Those holes are called a honeycomb," said Buzzby. "Each sister gets her very own little room."

"But all these new baby bees need food," said the queen. "And that food is honey. Buzzby, why don't you show our friends how we find flowers?"

Buzzby's wings buzzed with excitement. "Great idea! Follow me, you two. Time to meet a scout bee!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Wiggle Dance
chapters.text:
On a flat golden wall, a bee was wiggling in a funny little dance. She shook and walked in a circle, over and over.

Nell burst out laughing. "Why is she wiggling?!"

"That's a waggle dance," said Buzzby. "When a scout bee finds yummy flowers, she comes home and dances to tell everyone where they are."

Finn frowned. "Dancing tells them where flowers are?"

"The way she wiggles shows the other bees which way to fly, and how far," said Buzzby. "Watch her. Which way is she pointing, Nell?"

Nell watched closely. The bee wiggled up and to the left, over and over.

"That way!" Nell said, pointing up and to the left.

"PERFECT!" said Buzzby. "You just read a waggle dance! Flowers are that way, a little bit far."

A dozen bees buzzed up, watching the same dance. Then, one by one, they zoomed off in the exact direction Nell had pointed.

"They're all going because of you!" Finn said.

Nell beamed. "I'm basically a bee now."

"Not quite," laughed Buzzby. "But close! Let's follow them. Time to see nectar collecting."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: A Field of Yellow
chapters.text:
WHOOOSH! They flew out of the hive and into a field. Bright yellow flowers stretched everywhere.

"My favorite color!" Nell cheered, spinning around.

A fuzzy bee landed on a flower right next to them. She stuck out something long and thin, like a tiny straw.

Finn pointed. "What's that long thing?"

"That's her tongue," said Buzzby. "It's called a proboscis — a long tongue like a curly straw. She uses it to sip nectar."

"What's nectar?" Nell asked.

"Sweet juice inside the flower," said Buzzby. "Bees love it!"

Finn watched closely. "Where does the juice go?"

"Into a special pocket inside her, called a honey stomach," said Buzzby. "It's not for eating. It's just for carrying nectar home."

"Like a lunchbox!" Finn said.

"Exactly like a lunchbox," said Buzzby, giggling.

The bee buzzed from flower to flower, sipping and sipping. Yellow dust rubbed off onto her fuzzy legs.

"What's that yellow stuff?" Nell asked, pointing.

"Pollen," said Buzzby. "Flower dust. She carries it to the next flower, which helps new flowers grow."

Nell clapped. "So bees help my flowers?"

"They sure do," said Buzzby. "Now her tummy pocket is full. Time to fly home!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Mouth to Mouth
chapters.text:
Back at the hive, the forager bee met another bee waiting by the door.

"Watch this," Buzzby whispered.

The two bees touched their tiny mouths together. A tiny gold drop passed from one bee to the other.

"Ewww!" said Finn. Then he leaned closer. "Wait. That's actually kind of cool."

"Why don't they just keep the nectar themselves?" Nell asked.

"Teamwork," said Buzzby. "Passing it bee to bee helps change it. Their spit has tiny helpers inside it. Those helpers turn the sugar into something simpler, so it can become honey."

Finn scrunched up his nose. "So... bee spit is kind of magic?"

Buzzby laughed so hard her whole body buzzed. "Kind of! It's science magic."

Nell watched the nectar drop shine in the light. "It's turning gold already!"

"Not quite yet," said Buzzby. "But soon. This bee is about to pass it along one more time, to a house bee. She tucks it away."

The second bee flew off toward the honeycomb, the nectar drop glowing inside her.

"Can we follow her?" Finn asked.

"That's exactly where we're headed," said Buzzby. "Hang on tight, you two!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Six Little Sides
chapters.text:
They landed on a wall of small golden rooms, each one shaped the same way.

Nell squinted at one. "It has... one, two, three, four, five, six sides!"

"You counted perfectly," said Buzzby. "Those six-sided rooms are the honeycomb. Bees build them to hold nectar and honey."

"Where does the honeycomb come from?" Finn asked.

"We make it ourselves," said Buzzby. "Bees have special spots on their tummies that make wax. Soft, squishy wax, like candle wax. We build it into walls."

Nell poked a wall gently. "It's kind of bendy!"

"That's the wax," said Buzzby.

The house bee landed and spread her nectar drop into one of the six-sided rooms, smoothing it with her legs.

"She's tucking it into bed!" Nell said.

"Kind of," laughed Buzzby. "But it's not honey yet. It's still watery. There's one more step."

"What step?" Finn asked.

"Wings," said Buzzby. "Lots and lots of wings."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: A Tiny Windstorm
chapters.text:
Dozens of bees lined up next to the open rooms. They began to flap their wings, fast.

BZZZZZZZZZZZ! The sound got loud, like a tiny windstorm.

"Whoa!" Finn covered his ears, then grinned. "Can I help?"

He flapped his hands like wings. Buzzby giggled.

"That's sweet, Finn, but bee wings are much faster. They flap about two hundred times every single second. That's what makes our buzzing sound!"

"Two hundred?!" Finn flapped his hands as fast as he could. He only managed about ten. "I can't even get close!"

"Nobody can," laughed Buzzby. "That's why it's a bee job."

Nell watched the nectar drop in a honeycomb room. It looked thinner, then thicker, then shiny and golden.

"It's turning into real honey!" she said.

"All that fanning blows the watery part away," said Buzzby. "What's left is thick, sticky honey. Just like what's on Finn's toast!"

Finn gasped. "THAT'S why it's so sticky!"

Once the honey was ready, a bee walked over the little room. She sealed it with a thin cap of wax.

"Why cap it?" Nell asked.

"To keep it clean and safe," said Buzzby, "like a tiny lid on a tiny jar."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Twelve Bees, One Spoon
chapters.text:
"Why do bees work so hard for honey?" Nell asked, looking around at rooms and rooms of sealed gold.

"For winter," said Buzzby. "When snow covers the flowers, there's no nectar to find. Honey is our food that lasts and lasts."

Finn thought about the whole big field of flowers. "How much honey does it take to fill one tiny spoon?"

"A lot of work," said Buzzby. "It takes about twelve worker bees, their whole lives, to make just one teaspoon of honey."

Nell's mouth dropped open. "Twelve whole bee lives? For ONE spoon?"

"That's why we never waste a drop," said Buzzby.

"And it's not just food for you," Finn said slowly. "The yellow dust gets stuck on your legs. It goes to other flowers."

"That's pollen," said Buzzby, "and you remembered! That helps flowers make new seeds and new flowers. We help the flowers, and the flowers help us."

Nell looked proudly at her own yellow flower drawing, tucked in her pocket. "Teamwork."

"Even better," said Buzzby, "honey almost never goes bad, if it stays sealed up tight. Beekeepers gently take a little extra honey from hives like mine, and leave plenty behind for us."

Finn's eyes went wide. "Wait. Is that where MY honey comes from? The jar on our counter?"

Buzzby smiled her biggest smile. "Now you've got it, Finn. Every drop."

chapters.heading: Chapter 10: Home Again
chapters.text:
The golden light began to fade. "Time to go home," said Buzzby. "Hold on tight!"

WHOOOSH! The field spun away. The honeycomb shrank. The hive disappeared. Finn and Nell popped back through the tiny glowing door, growing bigger and bigger until they were just the right size again.

They stood in their own kitchen. The honey jar sat quietly on the counter, glowing one last soft gold, then going still.

Nell looked down. On the rug beside her yellow flower drawing sat one tiny, perfect honeycomb cell, no bigger than a button, shiny and gold.

"Buzzby left us something!" she whispered.

Finn picked up his honey toast. He looked at it like he'd never seen it before.

"Twelve bees," he said softly. "Their whole lives. For my toast."

Nell patted his hand. "Good thing you always finish it."

From somewhere far away, tiny and buzzing, they heard one last little voice.

"Buzz well, Finn! Buzz well, Nell!"

Then the kitchen was just the kitchen again, quiet and warm, and it was time for bed.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Finn. Goodnight, Nell. Buzz well.

true_facts.text: A **hive** can have up to **sixty thousand bees** living in it in summer.
The **queen bee** lays eggs — sometimes more than **a thousand in one day**!
A **scout bee** does a wiggly **waggle dance** to show other bees which way to fly to find flowers.
Bees sip sweet flower juice called **nectar** with a long tongue called a **proboscis**.
Nectar goes into a special **honey stomach** inside the bee, just for carrying it home, like a lunchbox.
Bees pass nectar mouth to mouth to their sisters back at the hive.
Bees spread nectar into the six-sided little rooms of the **honeycomb**.
Bees fan the nectar with their wings to dry it into thick, sticky **honey**.
It takes about **twelve worker bees**, their whole lives, to make just **one teaspoon** of honey.
Bees make honey to have food for **winter**, when there are no flowers to find.
The yellow dust called **pollen** sticks to a bee's legs and helps flowers grow.
**Beekeepers** gently take a little extra honey from a hive, and leave plenty behind for the bees.

new_recurring.name: Buzzby the Scout Bee
new_recurring.rule: Buzzby appears whenever the glowing honey jar hums and opens, and guides the children on bee or nature adventures, always signing off with 'Buzz well!'

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Finn and Nell returned to their kitchen to find a tiny golden honeycomb cell left on the rug, while the honey jar glowed once more before going still.

story.title: Omar and the Bicycle Bell
story.subtitle: A BMX bell rings backward through two hundred years of bicycles.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Bell That Glowed Green
chapters.text:
Omar was supposed to be asleep.

Instead he lay on his floor, BMX bike flipped upside down, spinning the front wheel with one finger. CLICK, CLICK, CLICK went the spokes.

Then the bell on his handlebar began to glow bright green and let out one soft chime.

**DING.**

Green light wrapped around him. **WHOOOOSH!** The floor dropped away.

Omar landed in a muddy field. A man stood by a strange wooden machine — two wheels, handlebars, a seat, but no pedals at all.

"Karl von Drais," the man said. "I built this in **1817**. My running machine."

"How do you go?" Omar asked.

"Push with your feet. Some call it a hobby horse."

Omar knew this move — like scooting a skateboard before popping up. He pushed off twice, lifted his feet, and glided smooth and straight.

Karl's jaw dropped. He tried it next — and tipped sideways into a haystack.

Omar laughed so hard he nearly fell too.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Boneshaker
chapters.text:
**DING.** The field melted into a cobblestone street.

A man knelt by a bike with pedals bolted onto the front wheel. No chain yet.

"Pierre Michaux," he said. "Try it."

Omar pedaled. The front wheel jerked with every push. CRUNCH, CRUNCH, CRUNCH went the cobblestones under him.

"This shakes my whole skeleton! People must call this a boneshaker!"

Pierre laughed. "Exactly right! Your friend **Pierre Lallement** even got a patent for it in the US — that means the government said the idea was officially his — back in **1866**."

Omar bent his knees low, like landing a big jump at the skate park, letting his legs soak up the bumps instead of his spine.

"Try that," he said.

Pierre wobbled off, knees bent, grinning. "Much better!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Taking a Header
chapters.text:
**DING.** Omar landed facing a bike so tall he had to tip his head back to see the seat.

"Penny-farthing," said a rider, climbing up with a running jump. "Named for two old coins — a big penny, a tiny farthing."

"Why so huge?" Omar asked.

"One turn of the pedals goes much farther. But stop too fast, and I fly right over the front — we call that taking a header."

Just then the front wheel hit a rock. The rider tipped forward.

Omar grabbed the handlebars. "LEAN BACK!"

He leaned, caught his balance, stayed up.

"Thanks!" he laughed. "Do you catch everyone at your skate park like that?"

"Just the wobbly ones," Omar said, grinning.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Safe One
chapters.text:
**DING.** A calmer street this time. A man rolled up on a bike with two matching wheels, low to the ground, a chain linking the pedals to the back wheel.

"John Kemp Starley," he said. "My Rover Safety Bicycle. Built it in **1885**."

Omar hopped on. It felt steady right away, nothing like that wobbly giant wheel.

"No headers?" he asked.

"No headers," John said. "Low, even wheels. Much safer."

Omar circled tight, then popped the back wheel up for half a second, just like at the skate park.

"IT'S SAFE!" he yelled, landing it clean.

John clapped. "That's exactly why the whole world copied it."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Bounciest Idea
chapters.text:
**DING.** Omar's teeth rattled — these tires were solid rubber, hard as a skateboard wheel.

A man knelt by a small tricycle, frowning. "My boy's ride is far too rough," he said. "I'm John Boyd Dunlop. I'm a vet — I look after animals — but I think I can fix this."

Omar looked at his own soft BMX tire. "What if you put air inside, like mine?"

John's eyes lit up. He wrapped a rubber tube around the wheel and pumped it full of air.

He pushed the tricycle. It rolled smooth and quiet.

"A pneumatic tire," John said. "Air-filled, **1888**. My name's still on tires today."

Omar bounced on his toes. "Smooth AND bouncy. Best combo ever."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Golden Age
chapters.text:
**DING.** Suddenly the street was packed with bikes, bells ringing, everyone laughing. The 1890s, and it seemed like the whole world wanted one.

A woman pedaled past, her long skirt drifting close to the chain.

"Watch your skirt!" Omar called.

She swerved it clear. "Good catch! That's why many of us wear bloomers now — loose, puffy pants that stay away from the gears."

"Bikes gave us somewhere to go, just us," she said. "All on our own, whenever we liked."

A voice nearby — **Susan B. Anthony** — called out, "Cycling has done more to set women free than anything else in the world!"

Omar nodded. "Pretty big deal for two wheels and some pedals."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Bicycle Shop
chapters.text:
**DING.** A small shop smelled of oil and metal. Two brothers bent over a bike frame made of thin, light tubes.

"Wilbur and Orville Wright," one said. "We fix bikes here in **Dayton, Ohio**."

Omar ran a finger along a spoke, thin but strong. "What else could you build with these?"

The brothers traded a look.

"Something," Orville said slowly, "we hope will fly."

Omar's eyes went wide. "Off the ground?"

"Same tricks," Wilbur said. "Light tubes, wheels with spokes. You'll hear about it in **1903**."

"Don't pedal too hard trying to take off," Omar joked.

Orville laughed. "Feet stay on pedals. For now."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Up the Hill
chapters.text:
**DING.** A long line of racers streamed by, legs pumping hard.

"The **Tour de France**," said a rider. "Started in **1903**. About **2,175 miles** across the whole country."

A hill rose ahead. Riders slowed, groaning.

"No gears yet," the rider huffed. "Those come later — a gadget called a derailleur that moves the chain so hills get easier."

Omar spotted a lever on a bike leaning nearby. "Is this one?"

"Try it," the rider said.

Omar clicked it. The chain hopped to an easier gear. He pedaled up without even standing.

"RING!" he shouted at the top, like ringing an imaginary bell.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back to the Skate Park
chapters.text:
**DING.** Dirt flew. Omar landed on a bumpy dirt track, bikes zooming over jumps.

"BMX bikes," said a rider, skidding to a stop. "Small and tough, built for tricks, like motorcycle racing but with pedals. Started here in the **1970s**."

"That's basically my bike!" Omar shouted.

Nearby, riders bounced down a rocky hill on bikes with huge, bumpy tires. "Mountain bikes," someone called. "Same decade — go anywhere, even dirt trails."

Omar grabbed a BMX bike by the fence and rolled to the top of a ramp. He'd landed this exact jump a hundred times at home.

He pedaled hard, hit the lip, spun clean through the air, and landed it.

The riders cheered.

**DING.**

Green light swirled. Omar landed back on his bedroom floor, wheel still spinning lazily under his hand. The bell glowed once more, soft green, then faded to plain silver.

He grinned at it in the dark. Every bike he'd ever ridden had come from somewhere — wood, pedals, big wheels, tiny wheels, all the way to his own.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Omar. Pedal on, and dream in wheels.

true_facts.text: Karl von Drais built a wooden two-wheeler called the running machine in **1817** — and it had no pedals at all.
People nicknamed it the hobby horse, and you steered it with handlebars just like a real bike.
In the 1860s, inventors bolted pedals straight onto the front wheel, making a bumpy ride called the boneshaker.
The penny-farthing had a giant front wheel and a tiny back wheel.
It got its name from two old coins — a big penny and a tiny farthing.
Riding a penny-farthing was risky — if you stopped too fast, you could tumble over the front, called taking a header.
In **1885**, John Kemp Starley built the Rover Safety Bicycle with two matching wheels and a chain.
In **1888**, John Boyd Dunlop made the first air-filled tire, giving riders a much smoother ride.
Long skirts were dangerous near bike gears, so many women switched to looser pants called bloomers.
In the 1890s, bicycles helped women travel on their own, and Susan B. Anthony said cycling set women free like nothing else.
Wilbur and Orville Wright ran a bicycle shop in **Dayton, Ohio**, before building the first airplane in **1903**.
The Tour de France bike race started in **1903** and covers about **2,175 miles** across France.
BMX bikes became popular in the United States in the **1970s**, inspired by motorcycle racing.
Mountain bikes with bumpy tires were invented in the 1970s too, built for riding down rough dirt trails.

story.title: Ada and the Magnet Robot
story.subtitle: A sticky, zappy bedtime adventure

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Fridge Magnet
chapters.text:
Ada lay on her bedroom floor, way past bedtime, building a robot face out of her fridge magnets on her little metal board. Eyes, nose, a big silly grin.

Then one magnet started to **hum**. It wobbled, popped off the board, and grew tiny arms and legs. "Beep! I'm Pip," it said. "Every magnet like me has two ends, a **north pole** and a **south pole**. That's where my pull is strongest."

Ada grabbed two magnets and turned them. One end snapped together with a **CLICK**. She flipped one around. It pushed away instead! "North likes south," Pip grinned, "but north pushes north away."

"I did that!" Ada said. "I flipped it myself!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Tiny Spinning Dots
chapters.text:
"Why do YOU stick," Ada asked, "and my wooden blocks don't?"

Pip's chest lit up like a tiny screen. "Inside me are teeny tiny bits called **electrons**. They spin around and act like mini magnets themselves."

"In me, they all point the same way, like soldiers lined up. That makes one big pull."

Ada pressed a wooden block against Pip. Nothing happened. "In wood," Pip said, "those tiny spinners point every which way, all mixed up. No team, no pull."

Ada tried a plastic spoon next. Nothing again. She grinned. "I bet metal spoons are different!"

"Try one and see," said Pip.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Invisible Push
chapters.text:
Pip floated up beside Ada's lamp. "Want to SEE my pulling power? It's called a **magnetic field** — the invisible space around me where I can push or pull."

He sprinkled tiny metal shavings onto a paper over himself. Ada gasped. They curved into loops, from one end of Pip to the other.

"Those little lines show the shape," Pip said. "Like a secret river only magnets can feel."

Ada traced the curve with her finger. "It goes round and round, not straight!"

"Exactly right," said Pip, bouncing happily. "You found the shape all by yourself."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Rock From Magnesia
chapters.text:
**WHOOSH!** The floor turned to dusty hills. "Welcome to ancient Greece," said Pip, "a very, very long time ago."

Ada spotted a dull gray rock lying near some iron nails. The nails jumped and stuck to it!

"That's **lodestone**," Pip said. "A magnet that grows right out of the ground. People here found it near a place called Magnesia. That might be where the word 'magnet' comes from — though nobody's totally sure!"

Ada held the rock up proudly. "I found the very first magnet!"

"You found A first magnet," Pip laughed. "Close enough for bedtime."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Pointer That Never Gets Lost
chapters.text:
Next, Ada stood in an old wooden boat, floating on paper waves. A sailor held a tiny floating needle.

"Over two thousand years ago," Pip said, "people in China used lodestones like this to make the very first **compasses**."

Ada poked the needle. It swung, then stopped, pointing the same way every time. "Why does it always point THERE?"

"Because Earth is one giant magnet," Pip said. "Swirling melted iron deep inside makes it so. The needle's north end gets pulled toward Earth's north."

Ada turned the needle every direction. It always swung back. "It's stubborn!" she giggled. "I like it."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Flip the Switch
chapters.text:
**BZZZT!** Sparks of light flickered — a junkyard, with a huge crane dangling a toy car.

"That crane uses an **electromagnet**," Pip said. "Wire wrapped in loops, with electricity running through. Turn it on, it pulls hard. Turn it off, it lets go."

"Doorbells use these too," Pip added, "and loudspeakers."

The crane buzzed, about to drop the toy car with a bang! Ada spotted the switch and flicked it OFF. The car lowered down soft and slow instead.

"Nice save," said Pip, impressed. "You stopped the crash yourself."

"Teamwork," Ada said, bowing like a tiny hero.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Snip the Magnet
chapters.text:
Back in her room, Ada eyed a long bar magnet on her desk. "What happens if you cut one in half?"

"Guess first," said Pip.

"Um... one half is all north, and one half is all south?"

Pip handed her safety scissors that couldn't actually cut metal, just for pretend. **SNIP!** Two shorter magnets appeared. Ada tested each end.

"They BOTH have a north and a south!" she gasped. "Two baby magnets!"

"Good guess, better discovery," said Pip. "Cut a magnet, and you just get more magnets."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back to the Fridge
chapters.text:
Pip led Ada home, right back to her little metal board. "One last test," he said, dropping a pile of spoons and rings in front of her. "A copper penny, a silver spoon, a gold ring, and this aluminum fork. Which ones will stick to a magnet?"

Ada held a magnet to each one. Nothing. Nothing. Nothing. Nothing.

"None of them!" she said. "Not all metal sticks?"

"Right," said Pip. "Only special ones, like the iron inside me, really love magnets."

Pip shrank down, glowing softer, and clicked back onto the fridge board as an ordinary magnet again. Ada yawned, pulled up her blanket, and smiled at her little metal friend.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ada. Stick together, and stay curious.

true_facts.text: A magnet has two ends called a **north pole** and a **south pole**, where the pull is strongest.
Matching ends push away, but a north end and a south end snap together.
Inside a magnet, tiny bits called **electrons** spin and act like little magnets lined up the same way.
When those tiny spinners all line up together, they make one strong pull.
In things like wood or plastic, the tiny spinners point every which way, so there's no pull at all.
The invisible space around a magnet where it can push or pull is called its **magnetic field**.
Tiny metal bits sprinkled near a magnet curve into loops, showing the shape of its pull.
A special rock called **lodestone** is a magnet that forms right in the ground, found long ago near a place called Magnesia.
More than two thousand years ago, people in China used lodestones to make the very first **compasses**.
Earth itself acts like one giant magnet because of melted iron swirling deep inside it.
A compass needle always swings to point north because it lines up with Earth's pull.
An **electromagnet** is made from wire wrapped in loops with electricity flowing through, and it can be switched on and off.
If you cut a magnet in half, you don't get a north piece and a south piece — each half becomes its own full magnet.
Not all metal sticks to a magnet: things like copper, gold, silver, and aluminum are not magnetic at all.

new_recurring.name: Pip the Magnet Bot
new_recurring.rule: A fridge magnet from Ada's own collection that glows, hums, and grows tiny arms and legs to guide her into science adventures, then shrinks back into an ordinary magnet when the story ends.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Ada falls asleep as Pip shrinks back into an ordinary fridge magnet, clicking softly onto her little metal board.

editor_notes: Give Priya a real beat in Chapter 7. For example, she could catch Newton's colour fan on her sunset drawing and name it, so the art-loving child is not offstage while Dev does the experiment.

story.title: Priya and Dev and the Rainbow in the Window
story.subtitle: A squirt, a sunbeam, and seven colors hiding inside a single raindrop.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Rainbow on the Wall
chapters.text:
Priya lay on her bedroom floor, drawing a sunset with her favorite orange marker. Dev knelt by the window, squirting his water pistol at the glass.

"I'm practicing my aim," he said, and squirted it again.

The last bit of sun turned the window gold. Drops on the glass caught the light. A tiny rainbow glimmered on the wall, right over Priya's drawing.

Then the little rainbow spun like a wheel. **POP!** A small glass triangle popped out of the light and floated in the air. "Hello," it said. "I'm Pip. I'm a **prism** — a clear shape that splits light into colors."

Priya sat up fast. "Did our wall just *talk*?"

"Rainbows need two things," said Pip. "Sun **behind** you. Water **in front** of you." Dev checked — the sun was behind the window, not behind him. He spun around, squirted his water pistol toward the glow, and — **WHOOSH** — the rainbow stretched wide and swallowed them both like a soap bubble.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Inside a Raindrop
chapters.text:
They landed with a soft **boing** inside something round and wobbly, like a giant water balloon.

"Welcome," said Pip, "to one single raindrop."

A beam of sunlight shot in, bent sideways, bounced off the back wall of the drop, and bent again on its way out. Dev watched it zigzag. "That's exactly like my squirt gun trick shot off the fence!"

"Light does the same bending trick," said Pip, "when it goes from air into water. It's called **refraction** — light slowing down and changing direction."

"So the raindrop is the fence," said Dev, grinning, "and the sunbeam is my water!" He pointed exactly where the light would pop out next. **CLICK** — right on target.

"Nice shot," said Priya.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Priya's Palette
chapters.text:
The bent sunbeam fanned out into a ribbon of colors, swirling around them.

"White light isn't just white," said Pip. "It's really **lots of colors mixed together**, and the raindrop sorts them apart."

Priya thought of her pencil case. "I always put mine in order — red, orange, yellow, green, blue, then purple."

"That's the rainbow's order too," said Pip. "Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. People remember it with the name **Roy G. Biv**."

Dev squinted at the swirling ribbon. "Why's red always on the *outside*?"

"Red bends the least," said Pip. "Violet bends the most, so it ends up on the inside."

Priya lined the colors up herself, matching her guess exactly. "Called it," she said, and took a bow.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Up for the Full Circle
chapters.text:
The raindrop popped, and they floated free in misty air, the whole rainbow curving beside them.

"It stops at the ground," said Dev. "That's kind of a short rainbow."

Priya tilted her head. "What if we went higher, like in a plane? Maybe there's no ground to stop it up there."

"Smart," said Pip. "Rainbows are actually **full circles**. We only see an arc because the ground blocks the bottom half."

Pip puffed up like a bubble and lifted them both. Higher, higher — and there it was, a complete glowing **ring** of color with nothing cutting it off.

"Whoa," said Dev. "It's a hula hoop made of rainbow!"

"People flying in airplanes sometimes see exactly that," said Pip.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Two Rainbows at Once
chapters.text:
Floating near the ring, Dev squinted upward. "Wait — is that a *second* rainbow? Way up there, all faded?"

Sure enough, a fainter arc glowed above the first one.

"Sharp eyes," said Pip. "That happens when light bounces **twice** inside some of the raindrops instead of once."

Priya looked closer. "The colors are backwards! Violet's on the outside this time."

"Exactly right," said Pip. "The second bounce flips the order."

Dev puffed out his chest. "I found a whole extra rainbow. That's basically a double scoop."

"Double scoop science," said Priya, nodding seriously, which made them both crack up.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: My Rainbow, Your Rainbow
chapters.text:
Pip set them down on two different clouds of mist, a few steps apart.

"Look at the arc now," said Pip. "Priya, where does yours start?"

"Right over that tree," said Priya.

"Mine starts over the *other* tree," said Dev, confused. "Did it move?"

"It didn't move," said Pip. "Every person sees their **own** rainbow, made from their own raindrops, because of where their eyes are standing."

"So I have a Priya rainbow and a Dev rainbow?" asked Dev.

"You've each got your own," said Pip.

Priya grinned. "Mine's obviously the better one."

"They're the *same* rainbow, show-off," Dev shot back, and they both laughed so hard the mist shook.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Newton's Trick
chapters.text:
Pip floated down and turned sideways, catching a sunbeam right through its own triangle body. A fan of colors spilled onto the mist.

"A scientist named **Isaac Newton** did this exact trick," said Pip, "back in the **1660s**. He shone light through a glass prism and proved that plain white sunlight secretly holds every color."

"Can *I* try?" asked Dev. He aimed his water pistol at a sunbeam and squirted a fine spray. Sure enough, a small rainbow flickered inside the mist.

"You just did Newton's trick with a water pistol," said Pip.

Dev puffed up proudly. "Sir Isaac Newton, squirt-gun division."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Chase for Gold
chapters.text:
"My cousin says there's **gold** at the end of a rainbow," said Dev, and took off running toward where the arc touched the ground.

He ran. The rainbow's end slid sideways, staying exactly as far away as before.

"That story might be a bit of a stretch," said Pip gently, "but lots of old tales tell it, especially in Ireland, about little leprechauns guarding gold."

Dev stopped, out of breath, hands on his knees. "It keeps *moving*!"

"A rainbow depends on exactly where you're standing," said Pip. "So you can never actually walk up and touch one."

Priya patted his shoulder. "No gold. But you did get some excellent exercise."

"Worth it," Dev panted, and they both grinned.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Home Again
chapters.text:
Pip gathered them up gently as the big rainbow began to fade. "Rainbows need sunlight *and* water droplets at the same time," Pip reminded them. "That's why they love showing up right after rain, when the sun peeks back out."

"They hide in other places too," Pip added, "waterfall mist, garden hose spray — even moonlight sometimes, though those ones are so faint they look almost gray."

"My water pistol is basically a rainbow machine," said Dev.

"Basically," Priya agreed.

**WHOOSH** — the rainbow shrank down to a glimmer, and they landed back on the carpet, right where they'd started. Pip shrank too, down to a tiny glass triangle, and settled on the windowsill, catching the last bit of light.

"Will you still be here tomorrow?" Priya asked.

"Whenever there's light to bend," said Pip.

Dev set his water pistol carefully by his bed, pointed at the window, just in case.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Priya. Goodnight, Dev. Keep looking for the colors hiding in the light.

true_facts.text: To see a **rainbow**, the sun has to be **behind you** and rain or spray has to be **in front of you**.
Rainbows often show up **after rain**, right when the sun peeks back out.
A rainbow forms when sunlight goes **into a raindrop, bends, bounces off the back, and bends again** coming out.
This bending is called **refraction** — light changes direction when it moves from air into water.
Plain white sunlight is really **lots of colors mixed together**, and raindrops sort them apart.
The rainbow's color order is always **red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet** — remembered as **Roy G. Biv**.
**Red** sits on the outside of a rainbow and **violet** on the inside, because violet bends the most.
Rainbows are actually **full circles**; we usually just see an arc because the ground blocks the rest.
People flying in **airplanes** sometimes see a whole **circle-shaped rainbow**, since there's no ground in the way.
Sometimes a fainter **second rainbow** appears above the first, with its colors **flipped backwards**.
Every person actually sees their **own personal rainbow**, made from different raindrops depending on where they stand.
In the **1660s**, scientist **Isaac Newton** used a glass **prism** to prove sunlight hides every color inside it.
Old stories, especially Irish tales, say there's **gold at the end of a rainbow** — but that part is just a fun legend.
You can never actually **walk up and touch** a rainbow, because it moves exactly as far as you move.

new_recurring.rule: A small glass triangle who appears out of bent or colorful light to guide the children through science adventures; speaks gently, loves a good light pun, and shrinks back into a keepsake at story's end.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: The adventure ends with Pip shrinking into a tiny glass triangle that settles on the bedroom windowsill, while Dev leaves his water pistol pointed at the window for tomorrow's light.

story.title: Jack, Ellie, and the Mermaid's Purse
story.subtitle: A bedtime dive through four hundred million years of sharks

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Pouch on the Carpet
chapters.text:
Jack dumped his beach bucket onto the carpet. Shells clattered everywhere.

Ellie held up a small, dark, leathery pouch. "Look! A mermaid's purse!"

Jack rolled his eyes. "Ellie. Mermaids aren't real."

"Neither are talking sharks," Ellie said. "But you still watch shark shows every night."

Jack grinned. She had him there.

Then the little pouch began to glow, soft green, like a nightlight under the sea. It hummed low and warm, like a seashell pressed to your ear.

"Jack," Ellie whispered. "Is it supposed to do that?"

"I don't know," he said. "But I want to find out."

The glow spread across the carpet, swirling into a window of blue light. WHOOSH! Cool, salty air rushed past their faces, though nothing got wet at all.

Through the window, long gray shapes glided by.

"Sharks," Jack breathed.

A gentle voice rose from the pouch, bubbling like it was speaking underwater. "Sharks have swum these oceans a very long time. Their skeletons aren't hard like yours. They're bendy, like the soft part of your ear. That bendy stuff is called **cartilage**."

Jack squeezed his own ear and grinned. "Whoa. Sharks are basically all ears."

Ellie giggled. "That's silly."

"It's true, though," said the voice. "Sharks were swimming around before dinosaurs ever walked anywhere. More than **400 million years** ago. That's older than trees."

Ellie's eyes went wide. "Older than Grandpa?"

"Much older," Jack laughed.

The window glowed brighter, as if it liked being asked questions. "There are more than **500 different kinds** of sharks swimming today. Want to meet some?"

Jack grabbed Ellie's hand. "Yes!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Tooth as Big as a Hand
chapters.text:
The light settled onto a quiet, sandy sea floor.

Something huge and white stuck up from the sand. A tooth, bigger than any tooth Jack had ever seen.

"Whoa," Jack said. "Is that from a shark?"

"It is," said the voice. "A giant shark called **Megalodon** swam here, millions of years ago. It isn't around anymore. Scientists say it's **extinct**, which means every single one is gone."

Ellie touched the tooth carefully. It was just old rock now, nothing alive.

"Why is there a tooth and no shark?" she asked.

"Shark skeletons are bendy, remember?" said the voice. "They don't turn to stone easily. Teeth are harder, so mostly what's left are old, rock-hard teeth called **fossils**. That's almost all we know about Megalodon."

Jack held his hand flat beside the tooth. It matched, fingertip to wrist. "It's as long as my whole hand!"

"Good eye," said the voice. "That's about right."

Ellie giggled. "Imagine brushing teeth that big."

"You'd need a mop, not a toothbrush," Jack said.

Ellie laughed so hard she snorted, which made Jack laugh too.

The sand shimmered, and the giant tooth sank away, leaving only a little ripple behind.

"Ready for something still swimming today?" asked the voice.

"Always," said Jack.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Gentle Giant
chapters.text:
A shadow slid over them, bigger than their whole house.

Ellie grabbed Jack's arm. "Is it going to eat us?"

"It's okay," said the voice quickly. "That's a **whale shark**. The biggest fish in the whole sea. It only eats tiny specks of food called **plankton**, smaller than a grain of rice."

Ellie peeked out from behind Jack's arm. The giant shark drifted by, covered in pale spots like stars on gray skin.

"It's... kind of pretty," she said.

"Over forty feet long," said the voice, "and gentle as a puppy."

Jack counted the spots near its gills. "How old is it?"

"Good question," said the voice. "Nobody can tell just by looking. But some whale sharks live to be **100 years old**, maybe more."

"That's older than Grandpa for real!" Ellie said.

Jack grinned. "Bet it's seen a lot of sunsets."

The whale shark swished its huge tail and glided off into the blue, unbothered, like it had somewhere calm to be.

Ellie waved goodbye, not too close, just a wave. "Bye, gentle giant!"

"You waved instead of swimming after it," said the voice. "Smart. Sharks like their space, same as you do."

Jack nudged Ellie. "See? Nothing to be scared of."

"I wasn't scared," Ellie said. "I was just... surprised."

"Sure you were," Jack teased, smiling.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Smile With a Thousand Teeth
chapters.text:
Something small and white drifted past Jack's nose.

He caught it in his cupped hands. "A tooth! Floating all by itself."

"That's from a **great white shark**," said the voice. "Great whites can grow up to **20 feet long**, with rows of sharp, pointy teeth for catching fish and seals."

Jack turned the tooth over. "Rows? Like, more than one?"

"Many rows," said the voice. "Sharks lose teeth all the time, and new ones just slide forward to take their place. Some sharks grow **thousands of teeth** over a lifetime."

Ellie's jaw dropped. "Thousands? The tooth fairy would be SO busy."

Jack burst out laughing. "She'd need a bigger pillow."

A real great white swam past in the distance, mouth closed, calm and unbothered. Jack watched, careful not to reach toward it. "We're just looking, right?"

"Just looking," agreed the voice. "That's how you visit a shark. Watch, don't touch."

Jack tucked the floating tooth safely into his pocket. "Souvenir."

"Lucky you found one that already fell out," said the voice. "Nobody had to go looking in its mouth for that."

Ellie laughed so hard she had to sit down on the glowing floor. "Good plan."

The shark swam off, unaware it had just become a bedtime story.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Hammer-Head Detective
chapters.text:
A strange shape appeared ahead, a shark with a head shaped like a hammer.

Ellie squinted. "That's... weird looking."

"That's a **hammerhead shark**," said the voice. "Its head is wide and flat."

"What's it for?" Jack asked.

"Its eyes are way out on each side," said the voice. "That gives it a view almost all the way around, like looking everywhere at once."

Jack held his hands flat against the sides of his head, like little wings. "Like this?"

Ellie copied him, hands wide. "I can see Jack AND the lamp at the same time!"

"Exactly like that," said the voice, sounding amused. "Hammerheads use that wide view to spot food hiding in the sand."

The hammerhead swung its head slowly side to side, then shot off after something small and silver.

"It found lunch," Jack said.

"Gross," said Ellie, "but also kind of cool."

"You have a hammer-head too," Jack teased, poking her hair. "A hammer-HAIR."

Ellie swatted his hand away, laughing. "You're the one with hammer-breath."

The hammerhead vanished into the blue, head still swinging, always looking.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Shark That Walks
chapters.text:
The water turned shallow, warm, and full of coral.

"Look!" Ellie pointed. "That shark's not swimming. It's... walking?"

A small, spotted shark pushed itself across the rocks using its fins, like tiny paddles.

"That's an **epaulette shark**," said the voice. "It can actually **walk** right across a reef using its fins, even out of the water for a little while. It doesn't need much air to do it."

Jack's eyes lit up. "Can we walk like it?"

"You can try," said the voice, laughing softly.

Jack and Ellie flopped onto their tummies on the glowing floor, paddling with their arms like fins.

"Left fin, right fin," Jack narrated, scooting forward.

Ellie scooted faster, giggling. "I'm winning the shark race!"

"No fair, your fins are shorter but faster!" Jack said, laughing so hard he could barely paddle straight.

The real epaulette shark waddled past them, unbothered, and disappeared over a ridge of coral.

"I think it won," Ellie said, out of breath.

"Rematch tomorrow," Jack said.

They collapsed in a giggling heap, coral light shining soft and blue around them.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Finding More Purses
chapters.text:
Tucked among the rocks, Ellie spotted something familiar.

"Jack! Look!" She held up a small, dark, leathery pouch, just like the one from her bucket.

"That looks like yours," Jack said.

"It IS a **mermaid's purse**," said the voice, warmly. "That's the nickname for a case some sharks lay their eggs in. A baby shark grows safely inside, tucked away like a tiny secret."

Ellie gasped. "So my purse... is a shark's egg?"

"It might have been, once," said the voice. "Not every shark lays eggs, though. Lots of sharks give birth to live babies, called **pups**, swimming and ready to go."

Jack grinned at his sister. "So this whole time, you've been carrying around a baby shark's old house."

Ellie looked at her pouch with new wonder. "That's actually really cool. Not gross at all."

"Not gross at all," Jack agreed. "Mermaid's purse. Shark's cradle. Same thing, I guess."

Ellie held the little case gently, the way she'd hold something precious. "I'm going to keep it forever."

The voice hummed, pleased. "Treasures like that are worth keeping."

Around them, more empty cases drifted gently in the current, little reminders that somewhere nearby, baby sharks were growing, safe and hidden.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Shark Lady and Going Home
chapters.text:
The light shifted once more, showing a woman swimming calmly beside a shark, her hand raised like she was giving directions.

"Who's that?" Jack asked.

"That's **Eugenie Clark**," said the voice. "People called her the **Shark Lady**. She studied sharks for years and years, and proved something important: sharks are curious. Some can even learn simple tricks, like coming when it's time to eat."

Ellie watched the shark follow the woman's hand calmly. "It's listening to her!"

"She showed the world sharks aren't just scary teeth," said the voice. "Sharks matter, too. They sit near the top of the ocean's food chain, which means they help keep everything else balanced, not too many of one fish, not too few of another."

"So sharks are kind of like ocean managers," Jack said.

"Pretty good way to put it," said the voice.

"But what if a shark tries to bite someone?" Ellie asked, a little quiet.

"That almost never happens," said the voice gently. "People hardly ever get hurt by sharks. Watching from a little distance, like you did tonight, is exactly how to visit them."

Jack nodded firmly. "When I'm bigger, I want to study sharks. Like her."

"I'll be the mermaid who tells them they're not scary," Ellie said, hugging her little leathery pouch.

The light began to dim, swirling gently from green to soft gold, back to the familiar glow of a bedroom nightlight.

WHOOSH. The carpet was just a carpet again. Shells lay scattered where they'd always been.

Ellie looked down at her hand. The little mermaid's purse was still there, dry and ordinary, resting in her palm like it always had been.

Jack found a tooth-shaped shell on the rug and tucked it into his pocket, right where the shark tooth had been.

"Same old room," Jack said.

"Same old room," Ellie agreed. "But I know way more about sharks now."

Jack yawned, suddenly heavy-eyed. "Tell me tomorrow if that was real."

"Tomorrow," Ellie said, already half asleep, hugging her purse close.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Jack. Goodnight, Ellie. Swim gently, and dream deep.

true_facts.text: A shark's skeleton isn't hard like ours. It's bendy, like the soft part of your ear — that stretchy stuff is called **cartilage**.
Sharks have been swimming the seas for more than **400 million years**, long before dinosaurs or trees.
There are more than **500 different kinds** of sharks swimming in the ocean today.
A giant shark called **Megalodon** swam long ago, but it's **extinct** now, meaning every single one is gone.
Shark skeletons rarely turn to stone, so almost everything we know about Megalodon comes from its giant **fossil teeth**.
The **whale shark** is the biggest fish in the sea, yet it only eats tiny bits of food called **plankton**.
Some whale sharks live to be **100 years old** or even older.
A **great white shark** can grow up to **20 feet long**, with rows of sharp, pointy teeth.
Sharks lose teeth all the time, and new ones slide forward to replace them, sometimes **thousands of teeth** in a lifetime.
A **hammerhead shark**'s wide, flat head spreads its eyes apart, giving it a view almost all the way around.
The **epaulette shark** can actually **walk** across rocks and reefs using its fins.
Some sharks lay eggs in a leathery case nicknamed a **mermaid's purse**, while others give birth to live babies called pups.
Scientist **Eugenie Clark**, called the **Shark Lady**, proved that sharks are curious and can even learn simple tricks.
Sharks hardly ever hurt people. Watching from a little distance, like Jack and Ellie did, is the safest way to see them.

new_recurring.name: The Mermaid's Purse
new_recurring.rule: A small glowing leathery pouch that hums and opens into a window of ocean light when a child asks it a real question; it speaks in a warm, bubbly voice, confirms correct guesses by glowing brighter, and always returns the children home…

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Jack and Ellie land back on their bedroom carpet with the glowing pouch now ordinary and dry in Ellie's hand, and a tooth-shaped shell tucked in Jack's pocket as a quiet souvenir of the night.

story.title: Nora and the Tile That Remembered Pompeii
story.subtitle: A night in a buried Roman town, one tile at a time

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Tile That Didn't Match
chapters.text:
Nora lay on her bedroom floor, tiles scattered around her like confetti. She was building a mosaic, a picture made from hundreds of tiny colored pieces fitted close together. It was late, way past bedtime, but the pattern wasn't finished.

One tile didn't match the rest. It was small, dusty, and dull red, nothing like her shiny glass ones.

She picked it up. It felt warm in her palm.

Then it started to glow.

"Finally," said a small voice. "Someone noticed me."

Nora nearly dropped it. "Did you just talk?"

"I'm a tessera," the tile said. "That's just a fancy word for one little mosaic piece. I used to be part of a floor in a Roman town. Want to see where I came from?"

Nora loved history. She loved mosaics even more. This was both at once. "Yes," she said. "Show me. Right now."

The tile glowed brighter. WHOOOOSH! Her bedroom floor melted away, and warm stone street appeared under her bare feet.

"Welcome," said the tile, "to Pompeii."

Nora looked around. Shops lined the street, their shelves stacked with clay jars. People in togas hurried past, carrying baskets and loaves of bread. Steam curled from a bathhouse doorway, and somewhere a dog barked.

"Where even is this?" Nora asked.

"Southern Italy," Tessera said, "near a city called Naples."

"It's busy," Nora said, counting doorways down the street. "How many people lived here?"

"Somewhere between **eleven thousand and fifteen thousand**," said Tessera. "Shops, bathhouses, theaters, temples — Pompeii had almost everything a town could need."

Nora grinned and spun in a slow circle, taking it all in. "It's like a whole city, just... really old."

"Really old," Tessera agreed, "and really alive, right now, in this moment."

Nora picked a direction. "Let's go that way," she said, pointing down a street with strange raised stones poking up from the ground. Tessera glowed approval, and they walked on together.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Dry Feet, Wet Road
chapters.text:
Nora stopped at the stones, raising an eyebrow. "Why are there rocks sticking up in the middle of the road?"

"Try stepping across them," Tessera said.

Nora hopped from stone to stone, careful not to touch the ground between. "My feet stayed totally dry!"

"Exactly," said Tessera. "Those are **stepping stones**. Romans used them to cross the street without stepping in mud or water. Carts still rolled through the gaps between the stones, wheels fitting just right."

"That's clever," Nora said. "Like a puzzle for feet and a puzzle for wheels, both at once."

Down the street, water trickled from a stone fountain built into the wall. Nora cupped her hands under it and felt the cold water run over her fingers. "There's water everywhere here."

"Pompeii had pipes running under the streets," Tessera said, "made of lead, carrying water to fountains all over town, so no one had to walk far."

Nora traced the fountain's edge with her finger. "So people didn't need to carry water from somewhere far away?"

"Not at all. They just walked to the nearest fountain and filled their jug," said Tessera.

Nora splashed a little water onto the stone, then hopped back across, counting this time. "Four across," she announced. "I bet kids used to race over these after school."

"Probably," Tessera laughed. "Where to next, Nora?"

Nora pointed toward a huge round building rising above the rooftops, its stone curve catching the sun. "There. That looks important."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Stone Bowl
chapters.text:
The round building loomed closer, its stone walls curving upward like a giant bowl turned on its side.

"What is this place?" Nora asked, stepping through a shadowy archway.

"The **amphitheater**," Tessera said. "A big stone arena, kind of like an ancient stadium, where crowds watched **gladiators** — fighters who performed here for a show."

Nora climbed the worn stone steps, running her hand along the smooth seats. "It's huge. How old is it?"

"Built around **70 BC**," Tessera said. "One of the oldest ones anyone has ever found."

Nora sat down on a sun-warmed step and looked out over the oval floor far below. "I bet it was so loud in here."

"Thousands of people came to watch," Tessera said. "Cheering, stomping their feet, probably shouting at their favorite fighters, just like at a game today."

Nora stood and stomped her own foot, once, twice, listening. The sound bounced around the stone bowl and came back bigger. "Whoa. It echoes!"

"The whole town could probably hear you," Tessera said, laughing.

Nora laughed too and counted the rows of seats as she climbed back down, losing count somewhere around twenty. "This place is older than almost anything I've ever touched in my whole life."

"Much, much older," Tessera agreed. "Ready to see what people wrote on the walls outside?"

Nora was already heading for the exit, practically skipping. "Lead the way."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Five Villages, One Town
chapters.text:
Outside, the wall beside the street was covered in painted words and scratched pictures, layer over layer.

"People wrote on the walls?" Nora asked, tracing a faded letter with her finger.

"All the time," Tessera said. "Some of it was advertising, like 'vote for this person' or 'come watch this show tonight.' Painted right on the outside, for everyone walking by to read."

Nora squinted at a faded word near the corner. "This looks like a name. Is it... Pompeii?"

"Good eye," Tessera said. "That's the town's name. Some people think it comes from an old word, **pompe**, meaning 'five.' Maybe because five little villages joined together to build one town, long before anyone painted a single wall."

Nora traced the number five in the air with her finger. "Five villages, one town. I like that. It's like five mosaic pieces making one picture."

She crouched and found a scrap of loose plaster on the ground, not part of any wall anymore, just a fallen piece. Underneath it was a swirl of blue paint.

"Even the trash has color here," she said, turning it over in her palm.

"Everything in Pompeii was painted," Tessera said. "Walls, floors, even ceilings, bright as anything."

Nora tucked the little chip of blue plaster into her pocket. "For later," she said. "Where next?"

Tessera's glow flickered, just slightly dimmer than before. "Next," she said, "is the day everything changed."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Mountain Across the Water
chapters.text:
The sky had turned strange — a thick gray smudge rising from a mountain far across the bay.

"What's that?" Nora asked, shielding her eyes.

"**Mount Vesuvius**," Tessera said quietly. "A volcano — a mountain that can blow out hot ash and rock. On **August 24th, in the year 79**, it erupted."

Nora's stomach tightened a little. "Is everyone okay?"

"Many people got away in time," Tessera said gently. "A young man named **Pliny the Younger** watched it from across the water and wrote it all down in two letters. He described it so carefully that scientists still call this kind of eruption a **'Plinian eruption,'** named after him."

"Like he was taking notes for later," Nora said.

"Exactly like that," said Tessera. "And his uncle, **Pliny the Elder**, sailed his ships straight toward the danger, trying to help people get to safety."

Nora watched the ash begin to drift down like gray snow, soft and silent. "It's actually kind of pretty. In a scary way."

"The ash fell for hours," Tessera said, "until it covered the whole town — as deep as **thirteen to twenty feet**. Pompeii went quiet, and stayed that way for a very, very long time."

Nora reached out and let a wisp of ash settle on her palm, then watched it vanish as the scene shifted. "What happened to it all, under there?"

"That," said Tessera, "is the best part."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Town That Fell Asleep
chapters.text:
The street around them shimmered, and suddenly they stood inside a small stone kitchen, dusty and dim, sunlight slanting through a gap in the wall.

"Where are we now?" Nora whispered.

"Centuries later," Tessera said. "This is what people found when they dug carefully through the ash, layer by layer."

On a stone counter sat a round loaf of bread, its crust still scored in neat lines from a baker's knife, sitting in an oven as if it had just come out.

"That's... bread?" Nora leaned close, careful not to touch it. "It still looks like actual bread!"

"The ash sealed everything so fast," Tessera said, "that bread, paintings, even writing on walls stayed just the way they were. We call that being **preserved** — kept safe, without rotting away, almost frozen in time."

On the wall nearby, bright colors still showed a painted scene of figures in a mysterious ceremony, reds and golds still glowing.

"That's beautiful," Nora said, stepping back to see all of it at once.

"That's a **fresco** — a painting made right into wet wall plaster while it's still soft," Tessera said. "This one is from a building called the **Villa of the Mysteries**."

Nora studied the brushstrokes, each one still crisp after everything. "Did this happen everywhere nearby, exactly the same way?"

"Not quite," Tessera said. "A smaller seaside town called **Herculaneum** got buried too, but under a different kind of ash. There, even wooden furniture and old scrolls survived, which almost never happens."

Nora touched the edge of the painted wall, careful not to smudge a thing. "It's like the whole town just fell asleep."

"That's exactly what it's like," said Tessera.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Dug Up, Piece by Piece
chapters.text:
The light shifted again. Now workers with shovels stood over a trench, brushing dirt gently from a stone wall.

"Who are they?" Nora asked.

"It's **1748**," Tessera said. "Workers digging here found old walls and objects, and realized a whole town was buried beneath their feet. That's when people started digging it up on purpose, instead of by accident."

Nora crouched beside the trench to watch. "Did they find it all at once?"

"Not even close," Tessera said. "Even now, only about **two-thirds** of Pompeii has been dug up. People who study old places carefully — we call them **archaeologists** — are still finding new paintings and rooms today, right now, somewhere under that ash."

Nora's eyes lit up. "So it's not finished? There's still more to find?"

"Still more," Tessera said. "Pompeii is so important now that it's a **UNESCO** site, which means a group that protects special places all over the world has promised to look after it. Millions of people visit every single year."

Nora stood and brushed imaginary dirt from her knees, grinning. "I want to visit. For real, one day."

"Maybe one day you will," Tessera said, her glow warming.

Nora looked back at the half-dug trench one more time, trying to picture it finished. "Thank you for showing me," she said quietly.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back on the Carpet
chapters.text:
The stone trench melted into carpet, and Nora blinked. She was back on her bedroom floor, tiles scattered just as before.

"Is Vesuvius still there?" Nora asked, turning the little tile over in her hand.

"Still there," Tessera said. "It's still an active volcano today. Scientists keep watching it carefully, because so many people live nearby now."

Nora nodded slowly. "Good. Someone should keep an eye on it."

She looked down at her half-finished mosaic, then reached into her pocket and found the little chip of blue plaster she'd picked up near the painted wall. She set it right in the middle of her pattern. It fit perfectly.

"Every tile tells a story," Tessera said softly, her glow dimming to a gentle flicker.

Nora smiled and set the tile carefully into its box, right beside her bed.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Nora. Every tile tells a story.

Pompeii's **amphitheater** was built around **70 BC**, one of the oldest ever found, where crowds watched gladiators.
Some outside walls were painted with ads and messages, like 'vote for this person' — an ancient kind of sign.
