story.title: Maya and the Porthole to the Stars
story.subtitle: A bedtime journey through the space race, with Barnacle the harbour seal.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Beep in the Porthole
chapters.text:
Maya lay on her bedroom floor, drawing a little sailboat in blue crayon, the paper curling under her elbow. A jar of brush-rinsing water sat beside her, cloudy and gray. It had been a whole week since the big bridge by the harbor finished humming its last beam into place, and Barnacle hadn't visited once since.

Then the water in the jar began to ripple, though nobody had touched it. A round brass window appeared right on her wall, swirling with water and tiny specks of starlight, exactly like the portholes on the fishing boats down at the dock. Two whiskers poked through first, then a familiar round, dripping face.

"All aboard, Maya!" said Barnacle, flippers dripping onto her carpet. "Tonight we're not going under the sea. We're going up — past the clouds, past the birds, past the Moon."

Maya scrambled to her knees, crayon still in hand. "Up where?"

"Space," said Barnacle, grinning his whiskery grin. "Listen first." A crackly beep came from the little toy radio on her windowsill, the one shaped like a ship's wheel. Maya turned the dial, chasing the sound, until it crackled in loud and clear: beep... beep... beep...

"That," said Barnacle, "is the sound of **Sputnik 1** — the first **satellite**, which just means a ball that circles around Earth up in space. The Soviet Union launched it on **October 4, 1957**. It was only about the size of a beach ball, and it sent out that very beep. People everywhere picked it up on their own radios, just like you did."

"BEEP, BEEP, BEEP!" Maya shouted, turning the dial louder still.

Barnacle flopped backward through the porthole with a happy SPLOOSH. "That's one small flop for a seal," he said, bobbing in the swirling water. "Climb through, Maya. The whole space race is waiting on the other side."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Ring Nobody Knew Was There
chapters.text:
On the other side of the porthole, Maya landed somewhere that smelled of hot metal and coffee. People in white shirts rushed past, clipboards in hand, all staring up at the sky like they were waiting for something.

"That little beep you heard surprised an entire country," Barnacle said, shaking water off his flippers. "The United States didn't have anything flying yet. So they built a brand new space team called **NASA**, which started its work on **October 1, 1958**."

On a table nearby, a model of the whole Earth spun slowly, glowing faintly blue. Maya leaned in close and spotted something strange: a thin, glowing ring wrapped clear around the globe, like a hula-hoop made of light.

"What's that?" she asked, tapping it gently with one finger.

Barnacle's whiskers twitched, pleased as anything. "Good eye. Nobody on Earth knew it was there — not until America's first satellite, **Explorer 1**, launched on **January 31, 1958**, and flew straight through it. It turned out to be an invisible ring of energy wrapped around our whole planet. Scientists had never once seen it before Explorer 1 found it."

"I found it first, this time," Maya said proudly, still tracing the glow.

"You did," Barnacle agreed. "Explorer flippers — I mean fingers — apparently run in the family."

Maya giggled and circled the ring all the way around the little Earth, like drawing a halo with one careful finger, while Barnacle hummed a tune that sounded suspiciously like a countdown.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: One Lap Around the World
chapters.text:
Red numbers glowed on a tall screen ahead of them: 10... 9... 8...

"Help me count, Maya," said Barnacle, flippers raised. She counted down with him, voice rising, faster and faster, until together they shouted, "ONE! LIFT OFF!"

WHOOOOSH! A silver capsule shot straight up through the porthole sky, trailing sparks of light.

"Inside that capsule," Barnacle said, "was a **cosmonaut** — that's simply the Soviet word for someone who flies in space. His name was **Yuri Gagarin**, and on **April 12, 1961**, he became the very first human being ever to leave Earth."

A toy Earth spun slowly on the table while a little bead of light circled it, once, all the way around. Maya watched closely, her finger tracking its path in the air. When the bead crossed back to where it had started, she shouted, "ONE LAP!"

"Exactly one lap," said Barnacle. "Gagarin circled the whole Earth once, in about **108 minutes**, and then came safely home again."

Maya sat back on her heels, amazed. "Who built the rocket that took him up there?"

Barnacle lowered his voice, like it was a secret worth keeping. "Nobody knew, for years and years. The chief rocket designer kept his own name completely hidden. He was called **Sergei Korolev**, and the world didn't learn his name until after he died, in **1966**."

"A secret genius," Maya whispered, eyes wide.

She picked up her crayon right then and drew him anyway — a quiet man nobody had ever gotten to draw a picture of before, his rockets scribbled tall behind him.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: A Bigger Dream
chapters.text:
A much smaller capsule bobbed nearby, barely bigger than a bathtub, bumping gently against the edge of the porthole scene.

"That one's American," said Barnacle. "On **May 5, 1961**, **Alan Shepard** climbed inside and became the first American in space. It was a quick flight — straight up, and straight back down. No full lap around Earth, not that time."

Maya watched the little capsule splash and bob and vanish. "That's it? That seems short, after one whole lap."

She breathed on the cold porthole glass until it fogged up white, then drew a circle with one finger — the Moon, with a tiny flag planted on top, just the way she liked to finish her boat drawings with a flag on the mast.

Barnacle's eyes went wide. "Funny you should draw that. Someone else had the very same big idea. On **May 25, 1961**, President **Kennedy** stood up in front of everyone and challenged his whole country to land someone on the Moon, and bring them safely home again, before ten years were up."

"Because a quick little flight wasn't big enough," Maya said, tapping her foggy drawing.

"Because a quick little flight wasn't big enough," Barnacle agreed. He patted her hand with one damp flipper. "Not bad, for someone still in pajamas. You just picked tonight's next stop, Maya."

Maya grinned and wiped the fog away with her sleeve, ready to go.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Factory Worker Who Flew
chapters.text:
The next capsule was shaped like an egg, and tiny — so tiny that when Maya climbed in just to look, her knees nearly touched her chin.

"Snug, isn't it?" said Barnacle, chuckling. A silver nameplate on the side read VOSTOK 6.

Maya traced the letters with one finger. "Was it only boys who got to go up, so far?"

"Not for long," said Barnacle, smiling his widest smile. "Meet **Valentina Tereshkova**. She used to work in a factory, before she trained hard to fly. On **June 16, 1963**, she became the first woman in space, orbiting Earth aboard this very capsule."

"She trained the same as anyone," Barnacle added. "Proof the sky doesn't care much where you started out."

Maya climbed back out and spun once in Barnacle's floating desk chair, pretending to circle the whole planet herself, giggling in dizzy circles until she very nearly tipped over sideways.

"Careful," laughed Barnacle, catching the chair with one flipper just in time. "Valentina had a fair bit more practice than that."

Maya steadied herself, still grinning, and tucked the thought away like a good smooth stone picked up off the beach — one she planned on keeping.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Floating on a Rope
chapters.text:
A hatch creaked open just ahead of them, showing nothing but black, scattered all over with stars.

Maya hesitated at the edge. "Isn't that scary? Floating out there with nothing around you?"

"It could be," said Barnacle gently, "unless you're holding on to something."

Maya thought of her swim lessons, how she held tight to a rope tied to a pool noodle so she never drifted too far from the dock. "He needs a rope!" she said suddenly. "Like my swim cord!"

Barnacle clapped his flippers together. "Exactly right. A cord called a **tether**. On **March 18, 1965**, a cosmonaut named **Alexei Leonov** opened that very hatch and became the first person ever to **spacewalk** — floating right outside his ship, tied on by a cord the entire time. He floated out there for about ten minutes before climbing safely back in."

"ALL TIED, ALL SAFE!" Maya cheered, and Barnacle cheered right along beside her, flippers slapping together.

Floating out in space, it turned out, wasn't so very different from floating in the deep end of the pool — just as long as somebody was holding the other end of your rope.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Look Behind You
chapters.text:
Through the porthole, a gray, dusty ball filled the whole view — the Moon, closer than Maya had ever once imagined it, every bump and crater showing plainly.

Everyone inside the little capsule stared straight ahead at it, cameras raised and ready.

"What's behind us?" Maya asked suddenly. "Nobody's looking back."

Barnacle turned, surprised by the question. Through the little rear window, a blue and white ball was rising slowly over the Moon's gray edge, bright against the black.

"Earth," Barnacle breathed. "In **December 1968**, the crew of **Apollo 8** became the first people ever to fly all the way around the Moon. One of them, **William Anders**, turned around just like you said, and took a photograph of Earth rising over the Moon's edge. They called it **Earthrise** — like a moonrise, only backward, with our whole planet doing the rising this time."

Maya grabbed her crayon and sketched it fast, right there on the fogged glass: a little blue marble, hanging just above a gray, bumpy horizon.

"You and Anders, both artists," said Barnacle, leaning in to admire her drawing. "Good eye, looking back when nobody else thought to."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Giant Leap
chapters.text:
The next rocket was so tall that Maya had to tip her whole head back just to see the top of it, a thin silver needle against the sky.

"That's the **Saturn V**," said Barnacle. "Three hundred sixty-three feet tall — taller than the Statue of Liberty. A team led by **Wernher von Braun**, who had built rockets before, designed it to carry astronauts all the way to the Moon and back."

Inside the porthole scene, a little silver lander drifted down toward a gray, dusty surface, wobbling side to side as it fell.

"It's coming in too fast," Maya said, and reached out with both hands, steadying the little model the exact same way she nudged her toy boat gently up to the dock at the harbor — slow, slow, easy does it. The lander touched down soft, and still.

"On **July 20, 1969**," said Barnacle quietly, "**Neil Armstrong** stepped out and became the first person ever to walk on the Moon. He called it 'one giant leap for mankind.' **Buzz Aldrin** climbed down after him, while **Michael Collins** stayed up above the whole time, circling alone in the command ship."

"ONE GIANT LEAP!" Maya shouted, jumping so high her socks left the carpet.

Barnacle laughed, delighted. "Close enough. Between **1969** and **1972**, twelve astronauts got to make that very same leap, across six separate landings. Seems to me you've just made one of your own."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: All Aboard for Home
chapters.text:
A light blinked red on a console nearby. Maya's stomach jumped.

"In **1970**," Barnacle said quickly, before she could worry too long, "a tank aboard **Apollo 13** blew while the crew was headed toward the Moon. It sounds frightening — and for a little while, it was — but clever engineers back on Earth figured out a fix, and the whole crew made it home safely."

Maya let out a long breath. "That's good. That's really good."

"It's very good," agreed Barnacle. "And capsules like that one always came down the very same way — splashing into the ocean, where ships were already waiting to scoop them right up."

He pointed below, where a wide blue sea spread out beneath the porthole. "Trouble is, it's an awfully big ocean to search."

Maya studied the water the way she studied tide charts with her dad, and pointed to one patch, darker and calmer than the rest. "There. That's where it'll land."

A tiny toy capsule dropped exactly where she'd pointed. SPLOOSH! A little recovery boat putted over at once and scooped it up, safe and dry.

"Got it in one," said Barnacle, deeply impressed. "That's the sailor in you, right there."

Then the water glowed gold all around them. "One more stop," Barnacle said. "On **July 17, 1975**, an American ship and a Soviet ship met way up in orbit, docked together, nose to nose, and the crews reached through and shook hands. After years of racing each other to be first, that's how the space race finally ended — with a handshake."

Maya reached out and shook one of Barnacle's flippers, solemn as anything for exactly two seconds, before she burst out giggling.

The porthole began to swirl, pulling them gently backward — back through stars, back through ocean, back to a small bedroom floor and a jar of paintbrush water, rippling softly now instead of plain.

Maya looked down at her old drawing of a little sailboat. Right beside it, without her quite remembering drawing it, sat a tiny rocket, pointed straight up at a paper Moon.

Barnacle's whiskered face appeared once more in the jar, dripping. "All aboard, Maya, for next time," he said, and sank back under, gone.

Maya pulled her blanket up to her chin and looked at her two little drawings side by side — a boat for the sea, a rocket for the sky.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Maya. All aboard, Maya, for dreams full of stars.

story.title: Zara and the Firestone Volcano Adventure
story.subtitle: A rock-solid journey through fire, ash, and a brand-new island.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Rock That Woke Up
chapters.text:
Zara sat cross-legged on her bedroom rug, lining up her rock collection by color. Red ones. Gray ones. One shiny black one that always felt warm, even in winter.

That black rock was a chip of real volcano glass. Grandpa called it the Firestone. Tonight, under her lamp, it did something it had never done before.

It started to glow.

Zara leaned close. "Firestone? Are you... awake?"

POP! A tiny orange light flickered inside the rock, like a spark caught in glass. A warm, crackly voice rose up. "Ready for a trip, Zara? I'm made from a real volcano. Want to see where I came from?"

Zara grinned so wide her cheeks hurt. "YES."

The Firestone glowed brighter and brighter, until her whole room filled with orange light. WHOOOOSH! The rug dropped away beneath her, and when the light faded, Zara stood on crunchy black ground under a smoky sky.

"Where ARE we?" she asked.

"Inside a volcano's story," said the Firestone. "A volcano is a hole in the ground where hot stuff from deep underground escapes. See that river over there?"

Zara pointed. Thick orange-red goo oozed slowly across the rocks, glowing like a nightlight. "It's so bright!"

"That's melted rock," said the Firestone. "Underground, we call it magma. Once it bubbles up and flows out where you can see it, we call it lava. Same stuff, different name."

Zara crouched near a cooled black rock, the kind that looked just like the Firestone. "Is this how you were born? From lava that went hard?"

"Exactly right," said the Firestone, glowing proudly. "You guessed it on your first try."

Zara tucked a little black pebble into her pocket, right next to her drawing notebook. "I'm going to find every kind of volcano there is," she announced.

The Firestone chuckled, a sound like popping embers. "Then hang on tight. There's a whole ring of them waiting."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Ring of Fire
chapters.text:
The ground gave a low RUMBLE, and Zara grabbed the Firestone a little tighter.

"Don't worry," it said. "That's just a little shake, far away. Watch this." The orange light spread out like a map, dotted with glowing spots all around a giant ocean.

Zara counted the dots circling the water. "There's SO many! Like a necklace of fire."

"That's exactly what people call it," said the Firestone. "The Ring of Fire. It's shaped like a horseshoe around the Pacific Ocean, and it holds about three out of every four volcanoes on Earth."

Zara tilted her head. "Why do they all live in one ring?"

"Good question. Earth's crust — the rocky skin on the outside of our planet — isn't one piece. It's cracked into giant puzzle pieces called plates. Most volcanoes pop up right where two plates meet."

Zara traced a finger along the glowing horseshoe. One cluster of dots was thicker than anywhere else. "This spot has WAY more dots."

The Firestone glowed with pride. "Sharp eyes. That's Indonesia. It has more active volcanoes than any country on Earth."

"Can we go there?" Zara asked.

"Not yet," said the Firestone. "First, let's visit a place that's not even on this ring at all — a place with volcanoes that break the rules."

Zara raised an eyebrow. "Volcanoes that break rules? I LIKE this already."

The orange light swirled, and the smoky ground melted away beneath her sneakers.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Hawaii's Gentle Giants
chapters.text:
WHOOSH! Warm wind hit Zara's face, smelling like campfire smoke. Waves crashed somewhere nearby, and the ground under her feet was smooth and black, like solid chocolate.

"Welcome to Hawaii," said the Firestone. "These volcanoes are rule-breakers, like I promised."

"Why?" asked Zara. "Aren't they on your ring thingy?"

"Nope. Hawaii sits over a hotspot — a spot where hot rock pushes up from deep below, right through the middle of a plate instead of at its edge."

Zara looked around at the gentle, rolling shape of the land. It wasn't steep and pointy like she'd pictured. It looked more like a shield lying flat on the ground.

"This doesn't look scary at all," she said. "It's kind of round and squishy-looking."

"You just described a shield volcano," the Firestone said. "Wide, with gentle slopes, just like Hawaii's. Not every volcano is a sharp, pointy cone like Japan's Mount Fuji."

Zara spotted a glowing orange crack nearby, bubbling steadily, like a pot of soup that never stopped simmering. "That one's still going!"

"That's Kilauea," said the Firestone. "One of the most active volcanoes on Earth. It's been erupting on and off for decades."

Zara looked past it to a much bigger, taller mountain in the distance. "And that giant one?"

"Mauna Loa. The biggest active volcano on the whole planet, over four thousand meters tall."

Zara whistled, a trick she'd just learned, and it came out a little squeaky. "That's SO tall!"

The Firestone laughed its crackly laugh. "Practice that whistle. We're going somewhere you'll want to make a much louder sound."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Day the Sky Turned to Ash
chapters.text:
The sky above Zara turned gray, then grayer, like someone had switched off the sun.

"Where are we now?" she asked, shielding her eyes.

"Italy," said the Firestone. "The year is 79. Watch that mountain."

Zara looked up at a huge mountain puffing a tall cloud of ash into the sky, stretching up like a tree made of gray fluff.

"That's Mount Vesuvius," said the Firestone. "It's erupting right now, covering two whole towns, Pompeii and Herculaneum, in thick ash."

Zara's eyes went wide. "Is everyone okay?"

"We're watching from far away, safe and sound," said the Firestone gently. "See that man over there, writing on a scroll?"

Across the bay, a man sat with paper and ink, scribbling fast while he watched the cloud grow.

"That's Pliny the Younger," said the Firestone. "He watched this whole eruption from a safe distance and wrote letters describing exactly what he saw. He wrote it down so carefully that scientists still use his words today. They even named this kind of huge, explosive eruption after him — a Plinian eruption."

Zara studied the strange shape of the ash cloud, wide at the top like a mushroom. "It looks like a tree," she said. "A gray tree in the sky."

"That's exactly how Pliny described it," said the Firestone, glowing warmly. "You just made the same observation he did, almost two thousand years later."

Zara beamed and copied the cloud's shape into her notebook, right next to her black pebble. "I want to write things down too, like him."

"Then you're already a scientist," said the Firestone.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Loudest BOOM in History
chapters.text:
The next WHOOSH dropped Zara onto a rocking boat deck, far out at sea.

"Cover your ears," said the Firestone, "just in case."

"In case of WHAT?" Zara asked — and then she heard it. A sound so loud it felt like it pushed against her whole body, even from far away. BOOOOOM!

"That," said the Firestone, "is Krakatoa, erupting in 1883."

Zara uncovered her ears slowly. "That was SO loud."

"It was the loudest sound ever recorded," said the Firestone. "People heard that exact boom about three thousand miles away, on a tiny island called Rodrigues. Imagine shouting in your backyard and someone hearing you all the way across the ocean."

Zara tried to imagine it and immediately started giggling. "My friends would never believe that."

"Most people didn't, at first," said the Firestone. "But sound can travel incredibly far when a volcano is powerful enough."

Zara pressed her ear to the deck, feeling a tiny rumble still humming through the wood. "I can still feel it!"

"Good ears," said the Firestone. "That's the sound of the Earth, still shaking from something that big."

Zara sat back, impressed. "I didn't know a sound could be a world record."

"Lots of things can be," said the Firestone, glowing with a little wink of light. "Ready for one that changed the weather for an entire year?"

Zara's ears perked up. "Wait, a VOLCANO changed the WEATHER?"

"Hang on tight," said the Firestone, and the deck dissolved into orange light.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Year Without a Summer
chapters.text:
Zara landed in a field, and something odd was happening. Snowflakes drifted down, even though the Firestone said it was summer.

"Is it supposed to snow in summer?" Zara asked, catching a flake in her palm.

"Nope," said the Firestone. "Not usually. This is 1816, and people called it the Year Without a Summer. Crops froze. Snow fell in June. It all traces back to one giant volcano the year before."

"Which one?" Zara asked.

"Mount Tambora, in Indonesia. In 1815, it had the biggest eruption ever recorded. It threw so much ash into the sky that it blocked some of the sun's warmth, all the way on the other side of the world."

Zara looked up at the gray, hazy sky above the snowy field. "One volcano did THAT? To a whole different country?"

"One giant volcano," confirmed the Firestone. "That's how powerful an eruption can be."

Zara scooped a little snow into a ball, testing it between her hands. "So this snowball... is kind of because of a volcano?"

"In a roundabout way, yes," said the Firestone, glowing with amusement. "You just connected a snowball in your hand to a mountain on the other side of the world. Not bad for a Tuesday."

Zara laughed and tossed the snowball gently into the air, catching it again. "Volcanoes are WAY more complicated than I thought."

"Wait until you see one that's still studied by scientists today, to keep people safe," said the Firestone. The field began to fade.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Mountain That Lost Its Top
chapters.text:
The ground beneath Zara trembled, steady and strong, like a giant drum.

"Where's the shaking coming from?" she asked.

"Washington State, 1980," said the Firestone. "Watch that mountain. Very carefully."

Zara stared at Mount St. Helens, its slope bulging strangely, like it was holding its breath. Then, with a groan, a huge chunk of the mountainside broke loose and slid downhill all at once — the biggest landslide ever recorded.

"WHOA!" Zara jumped back, even though she knew she was safe, watching from far away through the Firestone's glow.

The moment the side slid away, the mountain erupted sideways, blasting ash and rock into the sky. In seconds, about 1,300 feet of the mountain's very top was gone.

"That's enormous," Zara whispered.

"It is," said the Firestone. "A scientist named David Johnston was studying this volcano up close that very morning, working hard to understand it so he could help warn people when it was about to erupt."

Zara watched the ash cloud roll outward. "Did his work help?"

"It helped scientists everywhere learn so much more about how volcanoes behave before they erupt," said the Firestone. "Because people like him study carefully, many more people stay safe today."

Zara nodded slowly, tucking that thought away like a smooth stone in her pocket. "I want to study rocks that carefully someday."

"You're already halfway there," said the Firestone, glowing warmly. "Come on. Let's go somewhere a volcano didn't take a mountain apart — it built a whole new one."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: A Brand New Island
chapters.text:
Salty wind whipped Zara's hair as the ground re-formed beneath her — except this time, there was no ground yet. Just dark, churning ocean.

"Watch the water," said the Firestone.

Zara leaned over, careful not to get too close to the edge. Deep below the waves, something glowed. Then: BOOM. Steam and ash burst up through the water like an angry fountain.

"Is a volcano erupting UNDERWATER?" Zara gasped.

"It is," said the Firestone. "This is 1963, near Iceland. Keep watching."

Over the next moments, which the Firestone sped up like fast-forwarding a video, ash and rock piled higher and higher, until something broke the surface. A brand new island.

"It's being BORN!" Zara shouted, clapping her hands.

"Its name is Surtsey," said the Firestone. "A volcano built an entire new island, piece by piece, right out of the sea."

Zara tilted her head, thinking hard. "Why does Iceland get so many volcanoes, anyway?"

"Remember those giant puzzle pieces, the plates? Iceland sits right where two of them are pulling apart, slowly, making room for hot rock to rise up."

Zara clapped again, delighted. "So Iceland is basically ripping in half, SUPER slowly?"

"Exactly that slowly," said the Firestone, chuckling. "Slower than your fingernails grow."

Zara looked down at her own fingernails, painted lightly with glitter polish, and giggled. "That's REALLY slow."

"Ready for one more stop?" asked the Firestone. "The biggest volcano anyone has ever found — and it's not even on Earth."

Zara's eyes lit up. "Not on EARTH?"

"Hang on," said the Firestone, and the island faded into orange light.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Three Mount Everests, and Home Again
chapters.text:
The ground Zara landed on this time was dusty and red, under a sky with no clouds at all.

"Where are we?" she asked, looking around at the strange, rusty landscape.

"Mars," said the Firestone. "Look up. Way, way up."

Zara tilted her head back, and back, and back, until her neck hurt. A mountain rose in front of her, so tall it disappeared into a pink, hazy sky.

"That's Olympus Mons," said the Firestone. "The biggest volcano anyone has ever found, anywhere. It's about thirteen and a half miles high — almost three Mount Everests, stacked on top of each other."

Zara's jaw dropped. "THREE Mount Everests?!"

"Give or take," said the Firestone, glowing proudly. "Pretty great for a Tuesday, right?"

Zara giggled. "You keep saying that."

"Come on. One last stop, back on Earth, before bedtime."

The red dust swirled away, and Zara found herself standing near a small building with blinking lights and screens, somewhere green and ordinary.

"What's this place?" she asked.

"Where scientists watch volcanoes," said the Firestone. "They use machines called seismographs that feel even the tiniest shakes in the ground, and satellites in space that check if the ground is swelling up. Both are clues a volcano might wake up soon."

Zara peered at a screen showing a wiggly line. "It's like the volcano's heartbeat!"

"That's a wonderful way to put it," said the Firestone.

Outside, Zara noticed rows of bright green plants growing in dark, crumbly dirt near an old volcano. "Why's everything so GREEN here?"

"Volcanic ash breaks down into soil that's extra good for growing plants," said the Firestone. "That's why farmers often live near volcanoes, even knowing the risk. The ground is some of the best growing dirt on Earth."

Zara nodded, filing it away with everything else. "Volcanoes aren't just scary. They're kind of helpful too."

"Exactly right," said the Firestone, glowing its warmest glow yet. "Ready to go home?"

Before Zara could answer, the familiar orange light swirled up around her, warm as a blanket.

WHOOOOSH!

Zara landed back on her bedroom rug, rocks scattered around her exactly where she'd left them. The Firestone sat cool and quiet in her palm now, just an ordinary-looking black rock again, except for one tiny orange speck still glowing deep inside, like a tiny ember tucked away for next time.

Zara tucked it carefully onto her windowsill, right next to her favorite crystal. "Goodnight, Firestone," she whispered. "Rock on."

The little orange speck blinked once, like a wink, and went dark.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Zara. Rock on, dream bright.

true_facts.text: A **volcano** is a hole in the ground where hot stuff from deep underground escapes.
Underground it's called **magma**; once it flows out where you can see it, it's called **lava**.
The **Ring of Fire** is a horseshoe around the Pacific Ocean holding about three out of four of Earth's volcanoes.
**Indonesia** has more active volcanoes than any other country.
**Kilauea** in Hawaii has been erupting on and off for decades.
**Mauna Loa** is the biggest active volcano on Earth, over four thousand meters tall.
Hawaii's wide, gentle volcanoes are called **shield volcanoes**, shaped differently than tall, pointy ones like Mount Fuji.
In the year **79**, **Mount Vesuvius** erupted and covered the towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum in thick ash.
**Pliny the Younger** watched the eruption from far away and wrote it all down, so this kind of huge eruption is now called a **Plinian eruption**.
**Krakatoa's** 1883 eruption was so loud it was heard about **three thousand miles** away.
In **1815**, **Mount Tambora** had the biggest eruption ever recorded, and the next year became the **Year Without a Summer**.
The **Mount St. Helens** eruption in 1980 blew about **1,300 feet** off the top of the mountain.
In **1963**, a brand new island called **Surtsey** rose out of the sea near Iceland.
**Olympus Mons** on Mars is the biggest volcano ever found — about thirteen and a half miles high, almost three Mount Everests stacked up.

new_recurring.name: The Firestone
new_recurring.rule: A smooth black volcanic-glass rock from Zara's collection that warms up and glows orange to start an adventure, speaks in a warm crackly voice, and can open a window to real places and times to explore a science topic, always returning…

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Zara returns to her bedroom rug with the Firestone cooled in her palm, sets it on her windowsill beside her favorite crystal, and says goodnight as one last tiny ember glows and winks out inside it.

editor_notes: Fix the Atari 2600 claim. Say instead that its cartridges made swapping games popular, since the Channel F (1976) used cartridges first and the Odyssey already played several games.

Replace the Doom stop with an age-appropriate multiplayer moment, give Chapter 9 a single focus instead of three consoles in a row, and cut 'explained Miyamoto's own game back to him' or put Miyamoto in the scene.

Vary the repeated praise ('Good eye', 'grinning', 'Nice fix') and occasionally let Ben discover something rather than correct an inventor, so the fix-it formula doesn't wear thin. End the last chapter on a stronger line than the repeated 'I KNEW this place looked right.'

story.title: Ben and the Glowing Cartridge
story.subtitle: A pixel-powered trip through the history of video games

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Bouncing Dot
chapters.text:
Ben was building pixel-art Mario out of blocks in Minecraft. Square by square, way past bedtime.

His screen flickered. Green, then black, then green again.

A plastic cartridge dropped onto the carpet. It glowed like a firefly caught in a square.

"Whoa," Ben whispered, and picked it up.

A tiny pixel-shaped guy popped out of the glow, all blocky edges and a wide grin. "Name's Byte," he said. "Want to see where games came from? Hop in."

The carpet melted into a humming lab, full of wires and one round, glowing screen. A scientist leaned over it, fiddling with two knobs.

"That's William Higinbotham," said Byte. "He's got an **oscilloscope** — an old screen scientists used to see wiggly lines."

On the screen, a little dot bounced back and forth over a wobbly net-line.

"It's tennis!" Ben said. "But... weird tennis."

"Try the knob," said Byte.

Ben turned it. The dot zipped toward him on the screen and bounced right back. He turned it again, faster this time, and sent the dot flying past the lab's pretend net.

"POINT!" Byte yelled.

"In **1958**," said Byte, "Mr. Higinbotham built this at a place called **Brookhaven Lab**. Most folks call it the first video game anybody ever played."

"The graphics," Ben said, grinning, "are worse than my pixel art."

"Give the guy a break," said Byte. "He didn't even have blocks yet."

Ben turned the knob one more time, just to hear the dot bounce. BOOP. BOOP. BOOP.

"Okay," Ben said. "Where next?"

The lab spun away like a page turning.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Humming Giant
chapters.text:
They landed in a room that buzzed like a fridge the size of a bus.

"That," said Byte, "is a **PDP-1**. A computer so big, you could live inside it."

A college student named Steve Russell was hunched over it, tapping switches. On a round screen, two little triangle ships spun in slow circles.

Ben leaned close. "Those are spaceships. I can tell. I've drawn like a hundred of them."

"Good eye," said Byte. "This is **Spacewar!**, made in **1962** by Steve and his friends at **MIT**, a school full of computer nerds just like him."

One ship drifted too close to a blinking star in the middle.

"Wait," Ben said, pointing. "That star's pulling the ships in. Like gravity. He needs to spin away, not forward!"

Steve glanced over, surprised, and nudged the control. The ship swung wide and dodged the star.

"Nice call," Byte said. "You just out-piloted the inventor."

"I build spaceships in creative mode all the time," Ben said. "I just never had to dodge gravity before."

The two triangle ships traded little dots of fire, missing each other on purpose, looping and diving.

"No one's ever played a game like this before," Byte said. "You two just wrote the first chase scene in video games."

Ben laughed. "I'm putting this in my next build. Spinning spaceship, dodging a star."

"Add pixel art," said Byte. "Steve would've loved it."

The humming room folded away, triangle ships and all.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Box That Talked to TVs
chapters.text:
Next stop: a cluttered workshop, wires everywhere, and a plain brown box sitting on a workbench.

"Meet Ralph Baer," said Byte. "People later called him the **father of video games**."

Ralph plugged the box into a television. A white square blipped onto the screen and just... sat there.

"It's not doing anything," Ben said.

"That's the problem," said Ralph, rubbing his chin. "I want it to move when you push something. I just can't get the wires right."

Ben looked at the tangle of switches. It reminded him of wiring up redstone circuits in Minecraft — connect the right pieces, and something clicks to life.

"What if you don't need new wires," Ben said. "What if you just flip that switch there, the one you haven't tried?"

Ralph raised an eyebrow and flipped it.

The white square jumped sideways. CLICK.

"IT MOVED!" Ben shouted.

"This," said Byte, "became the **Brown Box**, built in the late **1960s**. A few years later, in **1972**, it turned into the **Magnavox Odyssey** — the very first game console you could plug into your own TV at home."

"So before this," Ben said slowly, "you could only play games on giant lab computers?"

"Exactly," said Byte. "Ralph brought it home. Literally."

Ralph shook Ben's hand. "Good eye for switches, kid."

"I've got a lot of practice," Ben said, "blowing up my own creations by accident."

Byte snorted. "Same energy."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Quarter Jam
chapters.text:
They popped into a noisy arcade — a room packed with glowing game machines you paid coins to play.

Two guys, Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney, stood proudly by a wooden cabinet. On its screen: two white paddles, one white ball. BOOP. BOOP.

"That's **Pong**," said Byte. "Nolan and Ted started a company called **Atari** and put this out in **1972**. Simplest game ever — and everybody loved it."

A line of kids had formed behind the machine.

CLUNK. The machine suddenly stopped. A kid pushed a quarter in. Nothing happened.

Ben crouched down and peeked into the coin slot. "It's jammed! There's like a hundred quarters stuffed in there!"

"Some people say," said Byte, "an early Pong machine once got so stuffed with quarters it actually broke. Might be a little exaggerated — but it shows you how fast people fell in love with this thing."

"I can fix it," Ben said. He found a little latch on the side, the kind he'd seen on toy coin banks, and popped it open. Quarters poured out, clattering onto the floor like rain.

The machine beeped back to life. BOOP. BOOP.

"NICE!" yelled the kid in line, and fed in a fresh quarter.

Nolan gave Ben a thumbs up. "Kid's got a future in repairs."

"Or arcades," Ben said, grinning, scooping up a handful of quarters just to hear them jingle.

"Put those back," said Byte. "They're not yours. Also, it's **1972**. Nobody takes IOUs."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Blocks That Swap and Aliens That March
chapters.text:
The arcade melted into another one, this time with a plastic box plugged into a TV.

"This is the **Atari 2600**," said Byte. "Came out in **1977**. Before this, a console only played one game, built right in. This one takes **cartridges** — little plastic cases with a whole game tucked inside. Pop one out, snap another one in."

Ben picked up a cartridge. "It's shaped like a chunky block. Kind of like Minecraft."

"You say that about everything," said Byte. "But yeah. Pretty much."

On the screen beside them, rows of little aliens marched sideways, then dropped down a line, then marched the other way.

"That's **Space Invaders**," said Byte. "Made in **1978** by a designer named **Tomohiro Nishikado**. It kicked off a huge arcade craze — everybody wanted to play it."

Ben watched the aliens for a second. "They always drop down right after they hit the edge. It's a pattern! Like mob spawns in Minecraft."

The player beside them was about to get hit.

"Move left, NOW!" Ben shouted.

The player ducked left just in time. The alien shot zipped past, missing by a block's width.

"Whew," Byte said. "Good read."

Ben held up the cartridge again and slid it into the console. CLICK. A brand new game lit up the screen.

"I love that it just swaps," Ben said. "Like changing worlds."

"Spoken," said Byte, "like a true gamer."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Pizza With a Bite Missing
chapters.text:
They landed somewhere bright yellow. A round little character gobbled dots down a maze, chased by four colorful ghosts.

"This one's **Pac-Man**," said Byte, "made in **1980** by a designer named **Toru Iwatani**."

Ben stared at the yellow shape. "It kind of looks like... a pizza. With one slice missing."

"Good eye," said Byte. "People say that's exactly where he got the idea — a pizza with a slice taken out. Nobody's totally sure, but it's a fun story."

On screen, Pac-Man zoomed into a corner, trapped, with two ghosts closing in.

"Left tunnel!" Ben called out. "It loops around to the other side!"

The player dove left. Pac-Man zipped through the side tunnel and popped out safe on the far edge of the maze, gobbling dots the whole way.

"That tunnel trick," Byte said, "not everybody spots that fast."

"I play a lot of mazes," Ben said. "Built like six of them in Minecraft."

A ghost caught up right as Pac-Man grabbed a big flashing dot. Suddenly the ghost turned blue and zoomed away, scared.

"HA!" Ben laughed. "Now HE'S running!"

"Big dot flips the chase around," said Byte. "Keeps things fair."

Ben watched the game loop a few more times, grinning the whole way. "I'm building a pizza maze tonight. With actual pepperoni blocks."

"Of course you are," said Byte.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Big Dig
chapters.text:
The next place smelled like dust. Store shelves sagged under piles of game boxes, way more than anyone could ever play.

"What happened here?" Ben asked.

"In **1983**," said Byte, "so many rushed, not-very-good games got made that people stopped trusting video games at all. Stores got stuck with boxes nobody wanted. The whole market in North America shrank way down."

"That's kind of sad," Ben said, looking at the dusty shelves.

"Yeah," said Byte. "But stick around. There's a wild part to this story."

The scene shifted to a dry, dusty stretch of desert in New Mexico.

"People used to say a truck came out here and dumped a bunch of unsold game cartridges into a giant **landfill** — basically a huge hole for trash — just to get rid of them," said Byte. "Including games about a certain movie alien."

"No way," Ben said. "That's just a story, right?"

"Grab a shovel," said Byte, "and find out."

Ben dug like he was mining in Minecraft, scoop after scoop. CLUNK. His shovel hit something plastic.

He pulled it up, covered in dirt. A game cartridge.

"IT'S REAL!" Ben yelled, brushing it off.

"In **2014**," said Byte, "real diggers came out here and found a whole pile of them, just like the story said. Turns out the legend was true."

"I'm a better miner than I thought," Ben said, grinning, dirt on his nose.

"Don't let it go to your head," said Byte. "You had a shovel from a magic cartridge. Slight advantage."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Jumping Plumber and the Falling Blocks
chapters.text:
They landed in a cozy room with a small gray console and a TV.

"**1985**," said Byte. "Nintendo brought out the **NES** — their new home console — here in the US, and it saved the whole video game business after the crash. It came packed with one very important game."

A little man in a red cap ran across the screen and hopped onto a floating block.

"That's **Mario**," said Byte. "Designed by **Shigeru Miyamoto**. He's probably gaming's most famous character ever — a jumping plumber."

Ben stood up and jumped in place, testing it out, like he was checking the controls himself. "The jump looks floaty. Like you're really controlling how high he goes."

He mimed tapping a button, short and quick. On screen, Mario hopped a tiny hop. Ben mimed holding it longer — Mario soared clean over a gap.

"That's exactly the trick," said Byte. "Press controls how high. You just explained Miyamoto's own game back to him."

On a second screen nearby, colorful blocks fell from the top, stacking up.

"That's **Tetris**," said Byte, "invented in **1984** by **Alexey Pajitnov**, a scientist in Moscow. Just falling blocks — and it's ridiculously fun."

Ben watched a row almost fill up, one gap left. "That one! The long skinny one fits right there!"

The long block dropped. SLOT. The whole row vanished. CLEAR!

"Oh, I'm good at this," Ben said. "It's basically Minecraft building, but faster."

"And with way less digging," Byte said. "For once."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Speed, Discs, and Plugged-In Friends
chapters.text:
A blue blur zipped past them so fast Ben felt the wind of it.

"Meet **Sonic**," said Byte. "Sega's speedy blue hedgehog, released in **1991**, made to race against Mario's popularity."

"He's basically Mario on zoomies," Ben said, watching Sonic loop a corkscrew track in a blur of spikes and rings.

Next to them, a different console glowed — this one spinning a shiny silver disc.

"**PlayStation**," said Byte. "Sony's console, from **1994**. It used CDs instead of cartridges, so games could have way fuller sound and video."

In the next room, rows of computers sat on folding tables, screens glowing, wires tangled everywhere.

"This game's called **Doom**," said Byte. "From **1993**. It helped make multiplayer matches huge — people hooking up a bunch of computers together to play against each other in the same room."

Ben looked at the tangled wires. "These cords aren't even connected right. Look — that one's loose."

He knelt down and plugged the loose cord firmly into place. The screens all flickered and synced up, showing the same glowing map.

"CONNECTED!" someone shouted from across the room.

"Nice fix," said Byte. "That's basically what we'd call a LAN party — everybody's computer linked up to play together."

"We do that with Minecraft servers now," Ben said. "Just, you know. Without the cords everywhere."

"Progress," said Byte. "Sonic still can't fix a cable to save his life, though."

chapters.heading: Chapter 10: Blocks All the Way Home
chapters.text:
The last stop felt different — brighter, more familiar. A console with a wand-shaped controller sat under a TV.

"The **Wii**," said Byte. "Nintendo, **2006**. You don't just press buttons — you swing the controller around like a real bat or racket."

Ben grabbed it and swung. On screen, a tiny cartoon version of him swung a tennis racket right back.

"That's so weird," Ben laughed. "I'm the controller."

The room shimmered again, and this time, blocky green hills stretched out in every direction. A familiar sun pixel-art-glowed overhead.

"Wait," Ben said slowly. "Is this—"

"**Minecraft**," said Byte, grinning. "Made by a Swedish developer named **Markus Persson** — everybody calls him **Notch** — back in **2011**. It ended up the best-selling video game ever made."

Ben spun around, grinning at the blocky world. "I KNEW this place looked right."

He reached down and placed one last glowing block on the grassy hill, right where he was standing.

The hills melted. The glow pulled backward, faster and faster, until —

Ben was sitting on his bedroom carpet again, Minecraft still open on his screen, pixel-art Mario half-finished.

The cartridge sat beside him, glowing softer now, almost sleepy.

"Same time tomorrow?" Byte's voice echoed faintly from inside it.

"Definitely," Ben whispered, setting the cartridge gently on his nightstand like a trophy.

He climbed into bed, dirt from the landfill dig still faintly on one finger, a smile stuck on his face.
chapters.shout_line: I KNEW this place looked right.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ben. Game on.

true_facts.text: In **1958**, a scientist named **William Higinbotham** made one of the first video games, a bouncing-dot tennis game shown on a round lab screen.
In **1962**, a student named **Steve Russell** and his friends made **Spacewar!** on a giant computer called the PDP-1.
**Ralph Baer**, later called the father of video games, built a game box for TVs called the **Brown Box** in the late **1960s**.
In **1972**, **Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney** started a company called **Atari** and released the arcade game **Pong**.
A fun story says an early **Pong** machine once got so stuffed with quarters it jammed up completely.
The **Atari 2600**, from **1977**, let players swap games in and out using plastic **cartridges**.
In **1978**, a designer named **Tomohiro Nishikado** made **Space Invaders**, starting a huge arcade craze.
In **1980**, **Toru Iwatani** made **Pac-Man** — some say the shape came from a pizza missing a slice.
In **1983**, too many rushed, not-very-good games flooded stores, and the video game business in North America shrank way down.
People used to say unsold game cartridges got buried in a New Mexico landfill — and in **2014**, real diggers actually found them.
In **1985**, Nintendo's **NES** console helped bring video games back, and it came packed with a very important game.
In **1984**, a scientist named **Alexey Pajitnov** invented the falling-block puzzle game **Tetris** in Moscow.
A developer named **Markus 'Notch' Persson** released **Minecraft** in **2011**, and it later became the best-selling video game ever.

story.title: Lena and the Ball That Remembered Everything
story.subtitle: A goalkeeper's tour through the history of soccer

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Ball Under the Bed
chapters.text:
Lena dove across her bedroom carpet for the ninth save in a row, gloves slapping the rug, elbow catching the beanbag chair.

It was an hour past lights-out. Her tennis-ball drill against the wall had gone from "ten more" to "fine, twenty."

On the twenty-first throw, the ball skidded under her bed — and came back glowing.

She reached in and pulled out something else entirely: an old leather soccer ball, scuffed brown, laced up the middle like a boot. It had not been there that morning.

The ball hummed. Then it spoke, in a crackly voice like an old radio. "Evening. Name's Whistler. You looking for a save, or a story?"

"Both?" Lena said.

"Good answer." The room folded sideways like a dropped blanket, and when it unfolded again, she was standing in a dusty courtyard full of shouting players in silk tunics, kicking a stuffed leather ball between two bamboo poles.

"Cuju," Whistler said. "A kicking game, played in China more than **2,000 years ago**. One of soccer's oldest known grandparents."

The ball sailed wide. Lena, pure instinct, dove and caught it on her fingertips before it flattened a vendor's stall.

The players froze — then roared, delighted. Nobody here used hands either, but nobody here had seen a save quite like that.

"SAVE!" Lena shouted, grinning, as the courtyard dissolved into light.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Game the King Banned
chapters.text:
The light cleared into a muddy English street, and chaos arrived with it.

Dozens of people — a whole town, it looked like — charged after an inflated animal bladder, shoving past market stalls, yelling over each other. Nobody wore a uniform. Nobody agreed on the rules, because there weren't any.

"This is called mob football," Whistler said. "No teams. No field. No fouls. The 'goal' is just the other end of town."

A cart tipped over. A window rattled. Lena ducked a flying elbow that wasn't aimed at her but might as well have been.

"This is a disaster," she said. "Somebody needs rules. Like — a field. Sides. No hands."

"Somebody will," Whistler said. "Eventually. In **1314**, it got so wild that **King Edward II banned it in London** altogether."

Lena watched the mess roll past — half soccer, half riot — and shook her head. "You can't play a game nobody agrees on."

"Hold that thought," Whistler said. "It's the whole rest of the trip."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Morley's Rulebook
chapters.text:
The next room smelled like ink and candle wax. A man in a stiff collar sat hunched over a notebook, crossing out words, writing new ones.

"**Ebenezer Cobb Morley**," Whistler said. "**1863**. London. He's about to write football's first real rulebook."

Lena leaned over his shoulder. Rule after rule, all arguments: Can you carry the ball? Can you trip someone? Morley kept crossing out "carrying" every time it came back.

"No hands," Lena said. "That's the one that matters. That's what makes it *this* game, and not rugby."

Morley looked up, startled, like she'd read his mind. He wrote it down: no carrying the ball. The room of men around him — the newly formed **Football Association** — voted yes.

"There's a schoolboy nickname going around for this new 'association football,'" Whistler said. "Shortened. Want to guess?"

Lena thought about it. "...Soccer? From 'assoc'?"

"Got it in one," Whistler said. "**1880s** England. Stuck forever."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: One Rule, One World
chapters.text:
A roar of a crowd, a cold gray sky, two teams lined up on muddy grass.

"**1872**," Whistler said. "Glasgow. Scotland versus England. The first official international match ever played."

Lena watched both goals stay empty the whole match — no slips, no scrambles, both keepers standing tall. "**0-0**," she said happily. "A clean sheet both ways. That's a keeper's dream game."

"Or a nightmare for the fans," Whistler said.

Decades spun past in a blur of new leagues and new countries, all playing by rules that had started in that one London room. A grand hall appeared, flags on the walls, officials shaking hands.

"**1904**, Paris," Whistler said. "Countries decide the game needs one world boss. FIFA gets founded. Guess how many countries signed up?"

Lena counted the flags on the table. "Seven?"

"Seven," Whistler agreed. "Little club. Huge job."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Uruguay, 1930
chapters.text:
Heat. Noise. A stadium packed to its iron rafters, flags everywhere, a ball bouncing down for kickoff.

"**1930**," Whistler said. "Uruguay. The very first World Cup."

Lena scanned the crowd — more flags for the home team than anyone else, the whole stadium painted sky blue. "Home team's about to win," she guessed. "Look at them. They *believe* it."

She was right. **Uruguay beat Argentina** in the final, and the stadium came apart with noise.

Afterward, an official carried out a small gold statue shaped like a woman holding a bowl above her head. Lena studied it.

"Who's it for?"

"**Jules Rimet**," Whistler said. "FIFA's president. The whole tournament was basically his idea. They named the trophy after him."

Lena turned the little statue over in her hands. "Heavy, for something so small."

"World Cups usually are," Whistler said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Dog Who Found the Cup
chapters.text:
London, decades later. A glass display case stood empty, its little velvet cushion bare.

"The **Jules Rimet trophy**," Whistler said, "got stolen right off this display. **1966**. Right before England hosted the World Cup."

Lena frowned at the empty case. "Someone has to find it. Dogs find stuff on walks all the time — they sniff everything on the ground."

"Funny you say that," Whistler said.

The scene shifted to a park, a man walking his dog on a lead. The dog stopped, nose down in some bushes, and would not move.

"A dog named **Pickles** found it, a week later, wrapped in newspaper," Whistler said. "Out for a walk — same as you guessed."

Lena pumped her fist. "FOUND IT!"

"England got its trophy back," Whistler said, "and then went and won the whole tournament. **1966**. Their only title, so far."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Three Stars and a Traffic Light
chapters.text:
Sunlight, green grass, a player in yellow weaving past four defenders like they were cones.

"**Pele**," Whistler said. "Brazilian forward. The only player ever to win the World Cup on **three** different squads — **1958, 1962, and 1970**."

Lena watched him glide past another tackle. "He makes it look easy."

"Brazil's won the whole thing **five times** total," Whistler said. "Nobody else is close."

A referee jogged past, reaching into his pocket for something colorful.

"**1970**," Whistler said. "A ref named Ken Aston needed a way to warn players without a language barrier getting in the way. He was stuck in traffic when it hit him."

Lena grinned. "Red for stop. Yellow for slow down."

"Exactly like that," Whistler said. "Yellow and red cards, debuting at this very World Cup."

"RED CARD!" Lena shouted, just because she'd always wanted to.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Lily Parr's Free Kick
chapters.text:
A packed stadium, but this time it was all women on the pitch, thundering through tackles in long skirts and wool socks.

"The **Dick, Kerr Ladies**," Whistler said. "One of the most popular teams in England. Their star forward was **Lily Parr**."

Lena watched her send a shot into the top corner, fans roaring. "She's incredible. Why haven't I heard of her?"

Whistler's voice went quieter. "Because the FA banned women's football not long after this. Said it wasn't suitable."

Lena's jaw tightened. "That's not fair."

"It wasn't," Whistler said. "But it didn't last forever. Want to work out when it ended? It was supposed to be for good — instead it lasted exactly fifty years."

Lena did the math out loud. "Fifty years later... **1971**."

"**1971**," Whistler confirmed. "Ban lifted. And twenty years after *that*—"

The scene shifted again: a packed stadium in China, women's teams battling for a trophy.

"**1991**," Whistler said. "The first official Women's World Cup. **The United States** won it."

Lena watched the celebration and felt, for the first time all night, like she was looking at her own future.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back Under the Bed
chapters.text:
The room folded one more time, and Lena landed back on her bedroom carpet, gloves still on, tennis ball sitting innocently by the wall.

The old leather ball sat beside her, laces glowing faintly, then not at all.

"That's the whistle," Whistler murmured, voice fading. "Half-time. Go sleep."

Lena picked up the ball and turned it over, the way she'd turned over a tiny gold trophy a thousand years and no years ago. On the leather, stitched faint and small, were two words she was sure hadn't been there before: *Eyes up.*

She set it carefully on her shelf, gloves still warm from a save that hadn't technically happened yet. Then she climbed into bed, already picturing tomorrow's drills.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, she had practice at six — and this time, she wasn't going to miss a thing.

true_facts.text: Cuju, a kicking game played in China more than **2,000 years ago**, is one of soccer's oldest known ancestors.
Medieval 'mob football' got so wild that **King Edward II banned it in London** in **1314**.
The **Football Association** was founded in London in **1863**, and banned players from carrying the ball by hand.
**Ebenezer Cobb Morley** personally wrote football's first rulebook in **1863**.
The word **'soccer'** comes from 'assoc,' a schoolboy nickname from **1880s** England.
The first **World Cup** was played in **Uruguay** in **1930**, where the host team beat Argentina in the final.
The original World Cup trophy was named after **Jules Rimet**, the FIFA president who helped create the tournament.
In **1966**, the World Cup trophy was stolen in London — and found a week later by a dog named **Pickles**.
**England** hosted and won the **1966** World Cup, its only title so far.
**Brazil** has won the World Cup a record **five times**.
**Pele** is the only player to win the World Cup on **three** different squads: **1958, 1962, and 1970**.
**Lily Parr** helped make the **Dick, Kerr Ladies** one of England's most popular soccer teams.
The FA's ban on women's football was finally lifted in **1971**, after fifty years.
The first official **Women's World Cup** was held in **1991**, and won by the **United States**.

story.title: Arjun and the Umpire of Sleep
story.subtitle: One cricket-ball nightlight, nine innings of science, and zero extra minutes.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Boy Whose Eyes Wouldn't Stop (1953)
chapters.text:
Arjun lay on his stomach, comic open under the blanket, flashlight gripped in his teeth. Five more minutes, he told himself. He always told himself that.

On the shelf, his cricket-ball nightlight — the one Dadi gave him after his first century — stopped glowing soft orange and flashed red instead.

"Five more minutes," said the ball, "is exactly what I was afraid you'd say."

Arjun dropped his comic. "You talk?"

"Only at bedtime. Call me Ump." The ball rose off the shelf and hovered like a dodgy umpiring decision. "Tonight we're reviewing something you do every single night and have never once watched. Sleep."

The room folded shut like a comic page turning. Arjun landed in a lab that smelled of chalk dust.

A young graduate student named **Eugene Aserinsky** was hunched over a sleeping boy, watching his eyelids twitch. Flick. Flick. Flick. His professor, **Nathaniel Kleitman**, stood behind him, arms folded.

"Why do his eyes keep moving?" Arjun whispered. "He's asleep."

"Watch the pattern," said Ump. "You track a ball better than anyone I know."

Arjun counted the flicks — steady, back and forth, like following a cover drive. "He's watching something. In his dream?"

"**In 1953**," said Ump, "Aserinsky and Kleitman proved exactly that. They called it **REM sleep** — Rapid Eye Movement. Your eyes dart because your brain is watching its own dream."

"THEY'RE WATCHING MOVIES WITH THEIR EYES SHUT!" Arjun yelled.
chapters.shout_line: THEY'RE WATCHING MOVIES WITH THEIR EYES SHUT!

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Ninety Minutes, Like a Session
chapters.text:
The page flipped and showed a wiggly line, up and down, up and down, like a run chart.

"That's your whole night," said Ump. "One full sleep cycle — quiet sleep, then dreamy REM sleep — takes about **ninety minutes**, start to finish."

Arjun, who knew his cricket sessions, did the math. "Eight hours is 480 minutes. That's over five cycles a night."

"Call it **about five**, give or take," said Ump. "Round and round, all night long."

In the dreamy part of the loop, a cartoon sleeper's arms twitched mid-swing, then flopped completely still.

"Wait, why'd he go all noodly?" Arjun asked.

"During REM," said Ump, "your brain is **almost as busy as when you're awake** — but your muscles go **limp**, like someone cut the power. So you can dream about hitting the winning six without actually kicking your brother out of bed."

Arjun grinned. "That explains a lot of mornings."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Growth Factory
chapters.text:
The next panel showed a door frame covered in pencil marks, each one a date, climbing slowly upward.

"Is this a growth chart?" Arjun asked, tracing the highest mark.

"Yours, probably, eventually," said Ump. "The deepest part of quiet sleep is when your body releases the most **growth hormone** — the chemical that helps you grow taller and stronger."

Arjun thought about the fast bowler he wanted to become. "So if I stay up finishing comics instead..."

"You trade height for pages," said Ump flatly. "Your choice. But the deepest sleep only shows up if you actually reach it."

Arjun shut his eyes right there in the panel, just to test the theory, and Ump had to physically roll him into the next page.

"Doesn't work that fast," said Ump. "Try again at home."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Body's Own Umpire
chapters.text:
The next page showed a glowing diagram of a brain, lit up like a stadium under floodlights. One dot shone brighter than the rest, tucked exactly where the nerves from both eyes crossed.

"That speck," said Ump, "no bigger than a grain of rice, is the **master clock**. Scientists found it sitting right there, over forty years ago."

"What's it do?"

"Same as me at a match," said Ump. "It watches the light coming in and calls when you should be awake and when you should be asleep."

Arjun squinted at a tiny sun symbol wired into the dot. "So light's basically its signal flag?"

"Exactly. There's even a word for your body's roughly one-day rhythm: **circadian** — Latin for 'about a day.'"

"MASTER CLOCK, MASTER CLOCK!" Arjun chanted, pointing, and for once Ump let him.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Three Names on One Trophy (2017)
chapters.text:
Next stop: a hall with a glass case, three photographs lined up like a top batting order.

"Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash, Michael Young," Arjun read. "A band?"

"Close," said Ump. "In **2017**, they won the **Nobel Prize** — science's biggest trophy — for finding the actual **genes**, the tiny instruction codes inside your cells, that keep your master clock ticking. Like gears inside the clock."

"So it's not just a dot. It's got machinery."

"Three scientists. One clock. Try saying that fast five times."

Arjun tried. He did not succeed.

"THREE SCIENTISTS, ONE CLOCK!" he shouted instead, which was easier and louder.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Dark Switch (1958)
chapters.text:
The comic page dimmed at the edges, like someone turning down a lamp.

"Why's it getting darker?" Arjun asked.

"Because your brain just noticed the room is darker," said Ump. "Back in **1958**, a scientist named **Aaron Lerner** and his team discovered the chemical your brain makes when it's time to wind down. They named it **melatonin** — the sleepy-time chemical."

"So darkness is the ON switch for it?"

"The off switch for you, the on switch for melatonin," said Ump. "Comics read under a flashlight are melatonin's natural enemy."

Arjun looked guiltily at the flashlight still clamped in his own teeth.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Filing the Day Away
chapters.text:
In the next panel, Arjun watched tiny versions of his own day get sorted into filing cabinets — a cover drive, a comic panel, the word circadian.

"Sleep does this every single night," said Ump. "It helps your brain sort the day into memories that actually stick — especially things you've been practicing."

Arjun thought about the shot he'd been working on all week. "So if I sleep well tonight, I might actually remember how I hit that six?"

"Better than if you stayed up re-reading a comic panel where you already know exactly what happens."

Arjun had no comeback for that one.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Eleven Days and One Bad Idea (1964)
chapters.text:
A grainy old photo showed a teenage boy, eyes propped open by sheer willpower, a newspaper headline floating above him.

"Meet **Randy Gardner**," said Ump. "**In 1964**, this seventeen-year-old from San Diego stayed awake for about **eleven days** — for a school science project."

"ELEVEN DAYS?!" Arjun's jaw dropped. "No five-more-minutes. Just none?"

"None. And doctors today say **never try it**. Going without sleep wrecks your mood, your focus, your memory, fast. Randy's experiment taught scientists plenty. It is not a trick to repeat."

Arjun nodded slowly, suddenly a little less proud of his own five-minute habit.

"Feeling better about bedtime?" asked Ump. "Then meet some professionals." The page flipped to a dolphin, gliding with one eye open, half its brain glowing. "**Dolphins** sleep with only half their brain at a time — one eye stays on watch."

Next, a giraffe dozed standing up. "**Giraffes** nap less than two hours a day, a few minutes at a stretch."

Then a bat, hanging upside down, utterly unconscious. "And some bats sleep **up to twenty hours**. Overachievers."

Arjun picked his favorite without hesitation. "The bat. Obviously."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back on the Shelf
chapters.text:
The comic page folded shut around him, and Arjun landed back on his stomach, blanket twisted, flashlight still between his teeth.

Ump glowed soft orange again, ball-shaped and quiet on the shelf.

"So," said Ump. "Five more minutes?"

Arjun clicked off the flashlight himself. "Nah. I've got cycles to run."

He set the comic on the nightstand, face up, right where he'd find it tomorrow — same page, same panel, waiting.

"Night, Ump."

"Well played, Arjun," said the ball, dimming to nothing.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow there would be five more pages to read — but tonight, the innings was over.

true_facts.text: In **1953**, scientist Eugene Aserinsky and his professor Nathaniel Kleitman discovered **REM sleep** by watching a sleeping boy's eyes twitch.
A full sleep cycle — quiet sleep then dreamy REM sleep — lasts about **ninety minutes**, and most nights run about **five** of them.
During REM sleep the brain is **almost as busy as when you're awake**, but your muscles go **limp** so you can't act out your dreams.
The deepest stage of quiet sleep releases the most **growth hormone**, the chemical that helps kids grow taller and stronger.
A speck of brain the size of a rice grain, called the **master clock**, sits where the eye nerves cross and controls sleeping and waking.
The word **circadian** comes from Latin words meaning **'about a day.'**
In **2017**, three scientists — Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash, and Michael Young — won the **Nobel Prize** for finding the genes that keep the body's clock ticking.
In **1958**, Aaron Lerner's team discovered **melatonin**, the chemical the brain makes to help the body wind down for sleep.
Sleep helps the brain **sort the day's moments into memories**, especially things you've been practicing.
In **1964**, seventeen-year-old **Randy Gardner** stayed awake for about **eleven days** as a school science project.
Doctors say **no one should ever try** to stay awake that long — it quickly wrecks mood, focus, and memory.
**Dolphins** sleep with only half their brain at a time, keeping one eye open to watch for danger.
**Giraffes** sleep less than two hours a day, in short naps while standing.
Some **bats** sleep up to **twenty hours** a day.
