story.title: Theo and the Dinosaur Update
story.subtitle: Player One loads a level 230 million years in the making.

chapters.heading: Level 1: Spawn Point, 230 Million Years Ago
chapters.text:
Theo was still awake at eleven-forty, which did not technically count as bedtime if the lights were off and the laptop was the only thing glowing. He had **Roblox Studio** open, building a new level the way he always did: one block, then ten blocks, then an idea that would not leave him alone until it was real.

It had been exactly one week since his screen had flashed a message that still sat folded in his notebook: THE NEXT LEVEL IS YOURS TO BUILD. He'd been building ever since, and so far nothing had happened. Tonight, something happened.

The screen went black, then green, then **BZZZT**. A small, square, unmistakably 8-bit green guy popped up on the taskbar like he'd never left.

"Player One," said Bit, "you have been building a very empty world."

"I'm still deciding what goes in it," said Theo.

"Then let's go find out what *used* to go on this planet," said Bit, "before either of us existed. Before anything with a face as cute as mine existed."

The laptop screen widened into a doorway, and the doorway was full of ferns the size of cars and a sky the color of an old bruise. Theo stepped through, because that is what Player One does, and the air smelled like wet rock.

"Welcome," said Bit, "to the very first level anyone ever built. Literally. This is where **dinosaurs** start."

Something small and quick darted between two ferns. Not huge. Not scary. About the size of a dog, if the dog had scales and an attitude problem.

"When?" said Theo, because that was always his first question.

Bit pulled up a loading bar made of glowing numbers. "Guess. I'll tell you if you're close."

Theo thought about every dinosaur documentary he'd ever half-watched while actually looking at his phone. "A hundred million years?"

"Bigger number," said Bit.

"Two hundred?"

"Closer. Try **230 million years ago**," said Bit. "That's the **Triassic period** — just a fancy name for the very first big chunk of dinosaur time. This little guy darting around is about as old-school as dinosaurs get."

Theo crouched to watch it go. It wasn't a T. rex. It wasn't anything from a movie poster. It was just small, fast, and first.

"That's it?" said Theo. "That's where the whole thing starts? One lizardy little guy nobody's heard of?"

"Every save file starts with one block, Player One," said Bit. "You should know that better than anyone."

A gold coin PINGED into existence and dropped into Theo's hand, warm and heavier than it looked.

"Level one," said Bit. "Complete."

chapters.heading: Level 2: The Man Who Needed a Better Word
chapters.text:
The next doorway did not have ferns. It had a cluttered desk, candle wax, and a man frowning at a pile of enormous bones like they owed him money.

"That," whispered Bit, "is **Richard Owen**. He has a problem. He has three different giant lizard-bones from three different scientists, and no single word for what they are."

The man set down a bone the length of Theo's arm, unsatisfied, and picked up another.

"'Big lizard' didn't sound very scientific," Bit said. "He needed something that meant business."

Theo looked at the bones: a jaw, a thigh, something with spikes. "What do they have in common?"

"They're old," said Bit. "They're reptiles. And they are, every single one of them, enormous."

Theo thought about it the way he thought about naming a Roblox game — something that told you everything before you even clicked play. "What if the name just said that? Old. Giant. Scary-looking lizard?"

Owen, as if he'd heard him, dipped his pen and wrote two Greek words on the page: *deinos*, terrible. *sauros*, lizard.

"In **1842**," said Bit, "Richard Owen put those two words together and made a brand-new one: **dinosaur**. It means '**terrible lizard**.'"

"That's it? That's the whole franchise name?" said Theo. "Somebody just smashed two Greek words together and it stuck for like two hundred years?"

"Good names last," said Bit. "You named your last level 'Lava Parkour But The Floor Is Rude.' People still play it."

Theo grinned. He couldn't argue with that.

Owen looked up suddenly, straight through the doorway, straight at Theo — or maybe just at the candle flickering in a draft that hadn't been there a second ago.

"Terrible," he murmured, trying the word out loud, "lizard."

A second gold coin dropped into Theo's palm.

"Level two," said Bit. "Complete. Also, legally, I would like it noted that I am not a lizard. I am 8-bit. There's a difference."

"BZZZT," said Theo, in Bit's own voice, and Bit made a sound like a dial-up modem laughing.

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Jawbone in the Quarry
chapters.text:
Bit's next doorway led to a limestone quarry in England, grey sky, men in flat caps, and a clergyman who looked far more excited about a rock than any clergyman really should.

"William Buckland," said Bit. "1824. He is about to do something nobody has ever officially done before."

"What, rocks?" said Theo.

"He's about to **name** a dinosaur," said Bit. "The very first one anyone ever named — officially, in print, with a title and everything."

Buckland was crouched over a jawbone half the size of Theo himself, lined with teeth like curved steak knives. He kept muttering a word Theo almost recognized.

"*Megalosaurus*," said Bit, before Theo could ask. "Big lizard. Not quite as catchy as 'terrible lizard,' but he got there first, in **1824**, before Owen even had a word for the whole group."

Theo leaned in toward the bone the way he'd lean toward a loading screen, trying to will it faster. "How do you even find a jawbone? Was it just lying there?"

"It took a while to get there," said Bit. "A **fossil** doesn't happen overnight. An animal dies, it gets buried fast — mud, sand, something that seals it in — and then, over thousands and thousands of years, minerals seep in and slowly turn the bone to stone. You're not looking at the original bone anymore. You're looking at a stone copy of it."

"So it's basically a save file," said Theo. "The animal's gone, but the data's still there if you know how to load it."

"That," said Bit, sounding genuinely delighted, "is the single best way anyone has ever described a fossil to me, and I have met a lot of **paleontologists** — the scientists whose entire job is digging up old bones and figuring out how the animal moved, ate, and lived."

A worker nearby was telling a story to another worker, something about a dog that dug up the very first piece of the jaw before anyone official got there. Bit caught Theo's eye.

"That dog story's been going around for a while," said Bit. "It's a good story. Nobody can actually prove it happened, so file it under legend, not fact."

Theo noticed something the men hadn't: a second, smaller curve of stone poking out of the quarry wall a few feet from the jaw, half-hidden under loose dirt.

"There's more of it," said Theo, pointing. "Right there."

Buckland's crew followed Theo's finger, dug where he pointed, and swore softly as more jaw came free of the rock.

"Nice find, Player One," said Bit, as a third gold coin dropped. "Level three. Complete."

chapters.heading: Level 4: The Girl on the Beach
chapters.text:
The quarry melted into a beach, grey cliffs, crashing waves, and a girl younger than Theo picking her way across slick black rocks with a hammer in her belt like it was the most normal tool in the world.

"**Mary Anning**," said Bit. "Born **1799**, in a town called **Lyme Regis**, on the English coast. By the time she's grown up she'll have found some of the most important fossils anyone found in her whole century."

The girl spotted something in the rock face, tapped it twice, and started working it free with a patience Theo did not personally possess for anything that wasn't a boss fight.

"Is that a dinosaur?" Theo asked.

"Great question," said Bit. "Go find out."

Theo scrambled closer, carefully, the way the game would have docked him points for falling off a cliff edge. The shape coming out of the rock had a long neck, flippers instead of legs, and a jaw full of pointy teeth.

"That's not a dinosaur," said Theo slowly. "Dinosaurs don't have flippers. I don't think. That looks like it lived in the water."

"Correct," said Bit. "That's a **plesiosaur** — a sea reptile that swam around at the same time dinosaurs were stomping around on land, but it's not actually a dinosaur. Neither is the flying kind — **pterosaurs** glide right over our heads in this level, and people mix them up with dinosaurs constantly, and it drives actual paleontologists up the wall."

"So dinosaurs were just the land ones," said Theo.

"Exactly. Sea reptiles, flying reptiles, dinosaurs — three different groups, all living at the same time, all getting lumped together by people who didn't do their research," said Bit. "You, Player One, are doing your research."

Mary worked the last of the skeleton free and sat back on her heels, grinning at it like Theo grinned at a build that finally loaded without crashing.

"She found stuff like this her whole life," said Bit. "On a beach most people only visited for the view."

Theo looked at the long rows of fossils already lined up against the cliff wall nearby — teeth, vertebrae, one skull Mary clearly hadn't gotten to yet. He pointed at the unopened one.

"That one's got a longer snout. Pretty sure that one's different again."

Bit checked. "You're right. Another sea reptile — a **mosasaur**. Also not a dinosaur. You're two for two."

The coin landed in Theo's hand already warm from the last one. "Level four," said Bit. "Complete."

chapters.heading: Level 5: Sue's Smile
chapters.text:
The beach vanished, replaced by red dirt, cracked and sun-baked, and a dig site roped off with little flags like the world's most intense capture-the-flag game.

"**South Dakota**," said Bit. "**1990**. Something's about to come out of the ground that is going to be a very big deal."

A woman on her knees was brushing dust off something enormous and curved, half-buried, pale as old ivory.

"Is that a tooth?" said Theo, already knowing the answer from the shape of it.

"That's a **Tyrannosaurus rex** tooth," said Bit. "And before you ask — yes, they're enormous. Up to **thirty centimeters** long, counting the root that was buried in the jaw. That's about a foot. One tooth."

Theo held his own hand up next to it for scale and immediately regretted it, because his whole hand didn't even cover it.

"This whole skeleton," Bit went on, "is one of the biggest, most complete T. rex skeletons anyone's ever dug up. They end up calling her **Sue**, after the person who spotted her sticking out of a cliff."

"How do you even miss something this big before now?" said Theo.

"You don't miss it," said Bit. "You just haven't looked in the right square mile yet. Ground this size takes forever to search."

Theo crouched by the skull, counting teeth along the jawline the dig team had already uncovered, losing track around twenty and starting over.

"These aren't even flat like a cow's teeth," he said. "They're curved. Like can-openers."

"That's exactly what a meat-eater's teeth are built for," said Bit. "Grabbing, not grinding."

One of the diggers, following the line of bone with a brush, stopped at a spot that looked, to Theo, suspiciously empty.

"There's a gap there," Theo said, pointing. "Right between those two ribs. That doesn't look right compared to the other side."

The digger frowned, checked, and called over a colleague — and sure enough, a rib had shifted out of place during the burial, exactly where Theo had spotted the mismatch.

"Nice eye," said Bit, as the coin dropped. "Level five. Complete. Sue, by the way, says hi. Probably. It's hard to tell with a skull."

chapters.heading: Level 6: Horns, Frills, and a Very Spiky Tail
chapters.text:
The doorway this time opened straight into a clearing, and Theo nearly stepped back out of it, because two dinosaurs the size of delivery trucks were standing nose to nose like they were about to start something.

"Relax," said Bit. "This isn't a fight. This is a **Triceratops** minding its business, and that over there is a **Stegosaurus** doing the same. Neither one wants trouble."

The Triceratops swung its head, and three horns caught the light — one over each eye, one on its nose — above a huge bony shield fanning out behind its skull like a collar built by someone who really did not want to get bitten on the neck.

"That's called a **frill**," said Bit. "Horns up front, frill in back. Fully loaded defense build."

The Stegosaurus, meanwhile, turned slowly, and its tail swung with it — a tail with long spikes on the end, swaying like a weapon nobody in their right mind wanted to stand behind.

"And that," said Bit, "is a **thagomizer**. Spiky tail, built for exactly one job: convincing anything hungry to reconsider."

Theo's brain did the thing it always did at a boss fight, started sorting stats. "So Triceratops is all front-line armor, and Stegosaurus is back-line damage."

"If you want to put it in game terms, sure," said Bit.

"I would absolutely build both of these as separate classes," said Theo, already half-thinking in Roblox Studio menus. "Triceratops tanks the hit. Stegosaurus punishes whoever's dumb enough to get behind it."

A low growl rolled out of the tree line, something neither armored plant-eater liked the sound of. The Triceratops lowered its horns toward the noise; the Stegosaurus turned its spiked tail toward it instead, covering the angle the horns couldn't reach.

"They're covering each other's blind spot," said Theo, watching the angles line up. "That's not an accident, right?"

"Nobody said it was," said Bit. "You just noticed it."

The growl faded back into the trees, uninterested, apparently, in two very well-defended dinosaurs. Theo let out a breath he hadn't noticed holding.

A gold coin dropped. "Level six," said Bit. "Complete. Nobody got eaten. Great level design, honestly."

chapters.heading: Level 7: The Turkey-Sized Surprise
chapters.text:
Theo had been waiting for this level since the trip started, and it did not look anything like he expected.

"Velociraptor," Bit announced, gesturing at a creature strutting through underbrush, "coming through."

Theo stared. It was about the size of a turkey. An actual, Thanksgiving-dinner-sized turkey, covered in what was unmistakably **feathers**, strutting around like it owned the forest floor.

"That's not — " Theo started. "That's supposed to be like, six feet tall with scales. I've played the games. I've seen the movies."

"Movies needed a bigger monster," said Bit. "Real Velociraptors were about **turkey-sized**, and these days most paleontologists think they were covered in **feathers**, not scales. Smaller and fluffier than their reputation."

Something glided overhead between two trees, not flying exactly, more like the world's best long jump, and landed on a branch with four wings spread out, two in front and two in back.

"That's **Microraptor**," said Bit. "Four wings. Could glide tree to tree. Looks like somebody's pet parrot had a very strange ancestor."

Theo watched it go, something clicking into place. "Wait. Feathers, wings, gliding — are you saying—"

"Birds," said Bit, "are what's left of the dinosaurs. That whole branch of meat-eating dinosaurs never actually went away — they just got smaller, grew better feathers, and started showing up at bird feeders. Every pigeon you've ever ignored is basically a dinosaur."

Theo looked at the little raptor, reassessed everything he thought he knew, and pulled up his mental image of the raptor boss he'd been building back home in Roblox Studio — six feet tall, scaly, roaring.

"I built mine completely wrong," he said.

"So fix it," said Bit.

Theo crouched by the real Velociraptor, studying the proportions, the feathers along its arms, the way it was built more like a fast, clever bird than a movie monster. For contrast, on the far side of the clearing, something the length of a basketball court was shaking the ground with every step — a long neck, legs like tree trunks.

"And that," said Bit, following his eyes, "is **Argentinosaurus**, maybe the biggest dinosaur there ever was, over a **hundred feet long**, give or take. So: turkey on one end, school-bus-and-a-half on the other. Same family tree."

"I'm redesigning the whole raptor level," Theo muttered, already picturing the edit. "Smaller model. Feathers. Make it fast instead of huge."

"That," said Bit, "is called research paying off."

The coin dropped, warm, into a hand already itching to get back to a keyboard.

"Level seven," said Bit. "Complete."

chapters.heading: Level 8: The Level That Isn't Finished Loading
chapters.text:
The last doorway didn't lead to a forest or a quarry. It opened on open sky, grasslands rolling to the horizon, and a stillness that made even Bit's pixels look a little subdued.

"This is the last level," said Bit. "**66 million years ago**. The end of the dinosaurs' long run — the non-bird ones, anyway."

"What happens?" said Theo, already bracing, the way he braced before a cutscene he suspected wasn't going to be fun.

"Most scientists think a giant **asteroid** — a huge chunk of rock from space — slammed into Earth, somewhere near what's now **Mexico**," said Bit. "It changed the whole planet's climate, fast. Most of the big dinosaurs couldn't survive the change."

Theo waited for the ground to shake, for something dramatic. Nothing did. The grass just moved in the wind, same as always.

"That's it?" Theo said. "No explosion? No—"

"We're not watching it happen," said Bit gently. "We're standing after. It already happened, a long, long time ago, and the world kept going. That's kind of the whole point of this level."

Bit gestured, and the scene shifted, not back in time, but sideways, to a nesting ground in what Bit said was modern-day **Montana**, rows of mud nests with eggs and small, clumsy hatchlings being fed by a parent twice the size of Theo.

"**Maiasaura**," said Bit. "The name means 'good mother lizard.' Scientists found whole nesting grounds like this one and figured out that at least some dinosaurs stuck around to take care of their babies, instead of just walking off."

Theo watched a hatchling stumble over its own feet and get nudged gently upright by its parent's snout. It did not look like the end of anything. It looked like Tuesday.

"And the birds," Theo said slowly, remembering. "They made it through. Theropods, feathers, bird feeders."

"Every sparrow owes its whole existence to that," said Bit. "Dinosaurs didn't disappear. They downsized."

One more image flickered past before the doorway home opened — a desert, golden and empty, stretching under a huge sky.

"**Gobi Desert**," said Bit, "Mongolia and China. One of the best places on Earth to still find dinosaur bones today. And over there—" a line of three-toed prints marched across hardened mud, frozen mid-stride for tens of millions of years, "—footprints. Whole trackways of them, still readable if you know how to look."

Theo crouched over one print, the size of a dinner plate, and set his own sneaker down beside it for scale.

"Somebody's still going to find more of these," he said. "Like, actual new ones. Tomorrow. Probably."

"Probably somebody is," Bit agreed. "That's the thing about this level. It isn't finished loading."

The doorway folded shut behind them, and Theo was back on his bedroom floor, laptop glowing, eight gold coins warm in his cupped hands. They rattled together, caught the light, and melted into each other, one shape, then another, until a small gold trophy sat in his palm: a Triceratops frill, a raptor feather, a single enormous tooth, all fused into one.

"Level complete," said Bit, and for just a second his pixel eyes looked suspiciously watery, glitching at the edges the way they always did right before a goodbye. "All eight. Nice work, Player One."

"Same time next week?" said Theo.

"BZZZT," said Bit, which Theo had learned by now meant *obviously*, and winked out.

Theo set the little gold trophy on his desk next to his keyboard, opened Roblox Studio one more time, and started deleting a six-foot scaly raptor model so he could build a turkey-sized feathered one instead.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, the raptor level was getting a very overdue rebuild.

true_facts.text: Dinosaurs first showed up about **230 million years ago**, in the Triassic period — the very first chunk of dinosaur time.
The word **dinosaur** means **'terrible lizard'** in Greek, put together by Richard Owen in **1842**.
**Megalosaurus** was the first dinosaur ever officially named, by William Buckland in **1824**.
A **fossil** forms when an animal's buried bone is slowly turned to stone by minerals, over thousands of years.
**Mary Anning**, born in **1799** in **Lyme Regis**, found amazing sea-reptile fossils on the English coast.
A **Tyrannosaurus rex** tooth could be up to **thirty centimeters** long, counting the root.
**Sue**, one of the biggest, most complete T. rex skeletons ever found, was dug up in **South Dakota** in **1990**.
**Triceratops** had three horns and a big bony **frill** to protect its neck.
**Stegosaurus** had a spiky tail called a **thagomizer**.
**Velociraptor** was really only about **turkey-sized**, nothing like its movie reputation.
Many Velociraptors are now believed to have had **feathers**.
**Birds** are considered the living descendants of meat-eating dinosaurs, so dinosaurs never fully disappeared.
Most non-bird dinosaurs died out about **66 million years ago**.
Many scientists think a huge **asteroid** struck near modern-day **Mexico**, causing that mass die-off.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Theo's eight gold coins fused into one small trophy, and he set it on his desk before opening Roblox Studio to rebuild his raptor as a smaller, feathered model.

scenarios.worst_moment: Orbit was barely three weeks old as a thing Americans could manage, and this man wanted the Moon within nine years.
editor_notes: Fix the Chapter 5 error. Americans could not yet orbit in May 1961, so make Eli's point that Kennedy set a Moon goal when the US had only managed a 15-minute suborbital hop, which is an even better 'insane' moment. Also stop Sputnik's beep spelling 'CCCP' in Morse, which misleads a physics-minded reader.

Break the dial-taps/Eli-explains/dial-confirms loop by letting Eli do things. He could retune the whisker to choose the next jump, test the orbit idea with a thrown object, or read the Explorer chart before the dial names it. That would also deliver the requested 'mysterious' tone if the Whisker Set's rules or origin became a puzzle he works at.

Pay off the paper tape by revealing its message, and trim the repeated tics ('filing it the way he filed', 'working it out loud', 'the way he always did'). Keep the dial's voice consistent: Morse capitals only, never quoted sentences.

story.title: Eli and the Radio That Remembered
story.subtitle: Ten frequencies, eighteen years, one very loud century.

chapters.heading: 1. Transmission at 1:14 AM
chapters.text:
The soldering iron ticked as it cooled on its stand. Eli had been awake for three hours past lights-out, trying to get the altimeter board on his model rocket to beep cleanly instead of screeching like a dying smoke alarm. On the desk beside him sat the other project: a shortwave radio built from parts that used to belong to his grandfather, its tubes glowing faint orange like a tiny campfire behind glass.

He wasn't even listening to it. That was the strange part. The radio wasn't plugged into anything he'd tuned — and it started beeping anyway. Not his altimeter's beep. A different one: steady, metallic, almost cheerful, like Morse code with nowhere to go.

*Beep... beep... beep...*

The dial, which had no business moving on its own, crept sideways until it stopped on a number with no station behind it. A voice came through the static, dry as a physics textbook and twice as amused. "Good. You're up. Most people sleep through the interesting part."

"Who is this?"

"Call me Control," said the voice. "You're listening to a signal that's sixty-some years old and still going. **October 4, 1957** — the Soviet Union puts the first man-made object into orbit. It's called **Sputnik 1**, and it's about the size of a beach ball, roughly **58 centimeters** across. No cameras, no instruments to speak of. Just a radio transmitter sending that beep you're hearing, simple enough that regular people around the world picked it up on ordinary radios like this one."

Eli frowned at the dial. "That beep's shifting pitch. That's not static — that's Doppler shift. The thing's moving toward us, then away."

"Because it's in orbit," Control said, sounding pleased, the way a teacher sounds pleased when you've skipped two steps and landed on the right answer anyway. "Want to hear what sixty thousand frightened, fascinated people heard that night? Tune it properly. You clearly know how."

Eli reached out and nudged the dial by feel, chasing the rising and falling pitch until it locked dead center. The beeping sharpened, filled the room, and the ceiling light flickered green. The garage seemed to fall away beneath him — not painfully, just like a held breath letting go.

When the static cleared, something that was not his garage stretched out around him: dark fields, a launch gantry lit by floodlights, and overhead, impossibly, a tiny bright dot crossing the stars on a schedule nobody on Earth had ever kept before.

"Welcome," said Control, "to the start of the Space Race."

chapters.heading: 2. The Dog Who Went First
chapters.text:
A month hadn't passed before the dial dragged itself sideways again. Eli, this time, was ready for it.

"Same frequency family," Control said. "Different payload. **November 3, 1957** — not even a month after Sputnik 1. The Soviets launch **Sputnik 2**. This one's carrying a passenger: a dog named **Laika**, the first living creature to go into orbit."

Eli had read enough rocket history to flinch slightly. "Did she—"

"She's remembered fondly," Control said, cutting gently ahead of the question. "Famous the world over. She proved a living thing could survive launch and get to orbit at all, which nobody actually knew for certain until she did it. That mattered more than almost anything else that year, because it meant a person might survive it too."

Eli stood at the edge of the vision — a launch pad, cold air, engineers in long coats double-checking a hatch — and thought about the physics he actually understood: the acceleration a launch puts on a body, the g-forces that could crush an untested assumption flat. "So she was the test pilot. Before anyone human got the job."

"Exactly that," said Control. "You're thinking like an engineer. Good. Space doesn't care how brave you are if the numbers are wrong first."

Eli reached out, not to touch anything — there was nothing to touch — but to trace the shape of the little capsule hanging in the vision's sky, small and lonely and first. For a second the beeping from the first chapter and the hum of this one overlapped, and he understood, in a way textbooks hadn't quite managed, that every giant leap starts with somebody — or something — going first, alone, before anyone knows if the plan survives contact with reality.

"Next stop," he said, and reached for the dial himself this time.

Control didn't argue. "Your radio now too, apparently."

chapters.heading: 3. A New Agency and an Accidental Discovery
chapters.text:
The next tuning took effort — the dial resisted, like it was climbing a hill made of static. Eli held it steady until it clicked.

"**October 1, 1958**," Control announced. "The United States, thoroughly rattled by a beeping beach ball, stands up a brand-new agency to get serious about space. They call it **NASA**."

The vision resolved into a cluttered control room, chalkboards covered in trajectory math that Eli actually recognized the shape of — parabolas, burn angles, the kind of thing his own rocket club argued about on Saturdays.

"Four months later," Control went on, "**January 31, 1958** — technically before NASA even opened its doors — the US launches its first satellite, **Explorer 1**. It's not much to look at. But its instruments find something nobody expected: a belt of radiation looping around the Earth, trapped by the planet's magnetic field. They name it after the scientist who spotted it in the data — the **Van Allen belt**."

Eli's eyebrows went up. "Wait — they weren't even looking for that?"

"They were counting cosmic ray hits with a Geiger counter," Control said. "The counts kept maxing out and going silent, over and over, which made no sense — until someone realized the instrument wasn't broken. It was *overwhelmed*. Too much radiation, not too little."

"That's not a discovery," Eli said slowly, working it out loud. "That's a malfunction that turned out to be the actual data."

"Most good discoveries are," said Control. "Nobody plans to find the thing. You plan to find the other thing, and the universe interrupts."

Eli grinned at that — it was, annoyingly, exactly the kind of thing his physics teacher would say, and exactly the kind of thing that made the subject worth losing sleep over. He turned back to the glowing chalkboard numbers, tracing one trajectory with a finger that passed right through the image, and felt, for the first time, less like a tourist in this story and more like someone standing in the room where it happened.

chapters.heading: 4. The Designer With No Name
chapters.text:
The fourth tuning didn't resolve into a launch pad at all. It resolved into darkness, a single lit window, and a man bent over blueprints nobody outside that room was allowed to see.

"This one's different," Control said, quieter than before. "This is **Sergei Korolev** — the chief designer behind the entire Soviet rocket program. Sputnik, Laika, everything you've seen so far. His work. His name."

"So why's it dark in here? Why's nobody saying his name out loud?"

"Because the Soviet government kept his identity a state secret," Control said. "The whole time he was alive, the public knew him only as 'the Chief Designer.' No photos released, no interviews, nothing. His name wasn't made public until after he died, in **1966**."

Eli stared at the man scratching figures into a notebook by a single lamp, the fate of an entire space program apparently resting on his sleep-deprived arithmetic, and no credit waiting for him on the other side. "That's — that's kind of brutal, actually. You do all that, and nobody's even allowed to know it was you."

"Meanwhile," Control said, the vision sliding sideways to a sunlit American hangar, "this is **Wernher von Braun**, who'd built rockets years earlier and later led the NASA team that developed the giant rocket you'll meet properly in a few chapters. Different country, different spotlight. Von Braun got magazine covers. Korolev got a locked door."

Eli looked between the two scenes — one lit, one hidden — and said what felt obvious once he'd said it: "So the whole race had two rooms like this, running at the same time, and neither one knew exactly what the other had figured out."

"That," said Control, "is the entire Space Race in one sentence. Well done."

The dial was already warming under Eli's fingers, impatient for the next stop.

chapters.heading: 5. The Dare
chapters.text:
The fifth frequency hit loud — cheering, a crowd, a man in a flight suit waving from an open car.

"**April 12, 1961**," Control said. "**Yuri Gagarin** becomes the first human being in space, aboard **Vostok 1**. One full orbit of Earth. About **108 minutes**, start to finish."

"A hundred and eight minutes to be the first person ever off the planet," Eli said. "That's shorter than most movies."

"History doesn't run on movie time," said Control. "Three weeks later, **May 5, 1961** — **Alan Shepard** becomes the first American in space, aboard a capsule called **Freedom 7**. Shorter flight, didn't orbit at all. Straight up, straight back down. Still counted."

The scene shifted again, this time to a podium, a president, a packed chamber. "And then, **May 25, 1961**," Control went on, "President Kennedy stands up in front of Congress and says the United States will land a man on the Moon and bring him home safely — before the decade is out."

Eli did the math without meaning to. "That's — they hadn't even managed a full orbit with a person yet. And he's promising the *Moon*. In eight years."

"Eight years, four months, and change," Control said. "Ambitious doesn't begin to cover it."

"It's insane," Eli said, and then, grudgingly, "It's also kind of the best kind of insane. You don't set a deadline like that unless you actually think the physics can be made to work."

"Can it?" Control asked, in the tone of someone who already knew the answer and wanted to hear a fourteen-year-old get there himself.

Eli thought about thrust and fuel and escape velocity — the speed you need to stop falling back down and actually leave — and shrugged, grinning despite himself. "Ask me again in a few chapters."

chapters.heading: 6. Forty-Eight Times Around
chapters.text:
The sixth tuning brought cold, bright sunlight and the hum of engines on a launch stand.

"**June 16, 1963**," Control said. "**Valentina Tereshkova** becomes the first woman in space, aboard **Vostok 6**. She orbits the Earth forty-eight times before she comes home."

Eli watched the capsule's thin white shape vanish into the sky and tried to picture forty-eight sunrises in a row, each one only ninety-some minutes apart, the planet turning underneath her window like a slow blue coin.

"She wasn't a pilot before this, was she," he said — half a question, half him remembering something he'd read once. "I think I heard she worked in a factory."

"She did," Control said. "Trained as a skilled amateur parachutist in her spare time, which is how she ended up on the Soviets' radar at all. Then they put her through cosmonaut training and sent her around the planet forty-eight times."

"So the qualification wasn't 'professional astronaut,'" Eli said slowly. "It was 'proven you can keep your head when you're falling out of the sky on purpose.'"

"Turns out that transfers," Control said, dry as ever. "Space doesn't check your résumé. It checks whether you panic."

Eli watched the tiny capsule arc up and out of sight, thinking about how much of this entire story, so far, had been exactly that — ordinary people, dogs, engineers kept anonymous by their own government, all of them betting that careful preparation beats raw fear. It was, he thought, a pretty good argument for doing your homework.

"Forty-eight times around," he said out loud, just to hear how big a number that actually was. "I've been around my own block maybe forty-eight times total."

"Different kind of orbit," said Control. "Same basic idea. You keep going because stopping is worse."

chapters.heading: 7. Ten Minutes Outside
chapters.text:
The seventh signal came in jagged, full of hiss, like something pressed right up against the microphone.

"**March 18, 1965**," Control said. "**Alexei Leonov**, aboard **Voskhod 2**, opens the hatch and becomes the first human being to leave a spacecraft while it's in orbit. The first spacewalk. About **ten minutes** floating outside, tethered to the ship, with nothing but suit and cable between him and open space."

The vision steadied into a view from outside the capsule itself — Earth curving away below, a figure in a bulky white suit drifting at the end of a line.

"Ten minutes doesn't sound like much," Eli said, then caught himself. "Except it's *everything*, isn't it. If that tether fails, or the suit fails, there's no air, no gravity to fall back toward, nothing. You're just — out there."

"He got back in fine," Control said, before the thought could go anywhere darker. "His suit stiffened up in the vacuum more than engineers expected, which made it hard to bend his way back through the hatch — so he had to bleed some pressure out of it just to fold himself small enough to fit. Not part of the plan. Worked anyway."

Eli exhaled, picturing it: the suit puffed stiff like an inflated glove, the hatch too narrow, ten minutes of silence turning into something closer to a math problem with a man's life as the variable. "That's not a spacewalk. That's an improvised repair on the fly, with the repair being *himself*."

"Most firsts are," Control said. "Nobody gets the procedure right the first time. They get themselves home, write it down, and the next person does it better."

Eli watched the tethered figure drift, safe now in the replay, ten minutes already folded into history, and thought that was probably the most honest description of engineering he'd ever heard.

chapters.heading: 8. The Picture That Changed the Argument
chapters.text:
The eighth tuning was quiet. No cheering crowd, no launch pad countdown — just the hum of a spacecraft and, through a small round window, a view Eli had seen a thousand times in photographs and had never once understood as something a person actually watched happen.

"**December 1968**," Control said. "**Apollo 8**. First crewed spacecraft to orbit the Moon. On one pass around the far side, astronaut **William Anders** looks up from his checklist and sees the Earth rising over the Moon's gray horizon — and takes the photograph."

Eli didn't say anything for a second. The Earth hung there in the blackness, small, blue, cloud-streaked, impossibly alone.

"It's called *Earthrise*," Control added, quieter. "First time most people on the planet had ever really seen the whole planet at once. Not a map. Not a globe in a classroom. The actual thing, from somewhere else."

"They weren't even supposed to be looking at Earth," Eli guessed. "They were supposed to be studying the Moon."

"They were," Control said. "The Earth coming up over the horizon wasn't on the checklist. Anders grabbed the camera because it was there and it mattered more than the checklist did, for about thirty seconds."

Eli thought about every photo he'd taken on his phone of something he hadn't planned to photograph — a rocket motor catching the afternoon light just right, a contrail bending the wrong way in the wind — and found, for once, that he understood exactly what had gone through that astronaut's head. You don't plan the best shot. You just don't put the camera down in time to miss it.

"Can we stay on this one a second longer?" he asked.

"Take your time," Control said. "It's waited fifty years. It can wait one more minute for you."

chapters.heading: 9. The Giant Leap
chapters.text:
When the ninth signal locked in, it came with a roar Eli felt in his chest before he heard it in his ears.

"**Saturn V**," Control said, as a rocket taller than anything Eli had ever stood near climbed off the pad on a column of fire. "**363 feet** tall. Taller than the Statue of Liberty. This is the rocket that gets Apollo 11 to the Moon."

Eli watched it go, doing the math on thrust and mass almost without meaning to, the way some people hum along to songs. "That's not a rocket, that's a building that decided to leave."

"**July 20, 1969**," Control went on, as the scene folded forward through days of silent travel to a gray, cratered plain. "**Neil Armstrong** becomes the first person to walk on the Moon. Calls it a giant leap for mankind on the way down the ladder. **Buzz Aldrin** follows him out a few minutes later. Their crewmate, **Michael Collins**, stays up above, alone, orbiting in the command module — a ship called **Columbia** — the whole time they're down on the surface."

Eli watched the small white-suited figures move in that strange slow bounce the low gravity gave them, and thought about Collins circling overhead, farther from another human being than anyone in history had ever been, with no one to talk to but Mission Control. "Collins doesn't get to walk on it at all. He just drives the bus and waits."

"Somebody has to," Control said. "Not every job in a first is the one that gets the headline. Most of the actual work never does."

Eli stood at the edge of the gray dust and the long black sky, close enough that it felt, for one unreasonable second, like he could reach down and pick up a rock himself. He didn't try. But he understood, more clearly than any textbook had managed, exactly how much had to go right — orbital mechanics, fuel margins, a thousand small decisions by a thousand careful people — for two boots to leave two prints in dust that had never been stepped in before.

chapters.heading: 10. The Handshake in Orbit
chapters.text:
The tenth signal came in rough, full of alarm tones that made Eli's stomach drop before Control even spoke.

"**1970**," Control said quickly. "**Apollo 13**. An oxygen tank explodes on the way to the Moon and cripples the spacecraft. I'll tell you the ending first, because you've earned it: every one of them gets home. Engineers on the ground spend days improvising a fix with whatever's actually on board, and it works. Nobody is lost."

Eli let out a breath he hadn't noticed holding. "Okay. Good. That's — okay."

"Between **1969** and **1972**," Control went on, steadier now, "across six successful landing missions, twelve American astronauts walk on the Moon. Twelve people, in three years, standing somewhere no one had ever stood."

The vision shifted one last time — no rocket, no gray dust, just two spacecraft, one marked in English, one in Russian, drifting slowly toward each other against the black.

"**July 17, 1975**," Control said. "American and Soviet spacecraft dock in orbit. Their crews open the hatch between them and shake hands, in space, after eighteen years of racing each other to get there first."

Eli watched the handshake happen, small and almost ordinary-looking after everything that had led to it, and found that was exactly what made it land. "So it doesn't end with somebody winning," he said. "It ends with both of them just — meeting in the middle."

"Best kind of ending a race like that can have," Control said.

The dial went dark on its own this time. The green light faded from the ceiling, and the garage came back around Eli piece by piece — the half-finished rocket board, the cold soldering iron, the ordinary hum of the refrigerator two rooms away. On the radio's speaker grille, where there had never been one before, sat a small printed card, warm to the touch, with a frequency written on it in neat block letters and nothing else.

Eli looked at it a long moment, then set it carefully beside his rocket board, exactly where he'd see it first thing tomorrow.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow there was a telemetry board to finish — and a new frequency waiting on the desk.

true_facts.text: On **October 4, 1957**, the Soviet Union launched **Sputnik 1**, the first man-made object to orbit Earth.
On **November 3, 1957**, the Soviets launched **Sputnik 2**, carrying a dog named **Laika**, the first living creature to orbit Earth.
**NASA** began operating on **October 1, 1958**, after the US was rattled by Sputnik.
The first US satellite, **Explorer 1**, launched **January 31, 1958**, and its instruments accidentally discovered a belt of radiation looping around Earth, now called the **Van Allen belt**.
The Soviet Union's chief rocket designer, **Sergei Korolev**, was kept a state secret — his name wasn't made public until after his death in **1966**.
**Wernher von Braun** led the NASA team that developed the giant **Saturn V** rocket.
On **April 12, 1961**, **Yuri Gagarin** became the first human in space, orbiting Earth once aboard **Vostok 1** in about **108 minutes**.
On **May 25, 1961**, President **Kennedy** challenged the US to land a man on the Moon and bring him home before the decade was out.
On **June 16, 1963**, **Valentina Tereshkova** became the first woman in space, orbiting Earth **48 times** aboard **Vostok 6**.
On **March 18, 1965**, **Alexei Leonov** made the first spacewalk, floating outside his capsule for about **ten minutes**.
In **December 1968**, the Apollo 8 crew became the first to orbit the Moon, and astronaut **William Anders** took the famous **Earthrise** photo.
On **July 20, 1969**, **Neil Armstrong** became the first person to walk on the Moon, calling it a giant leap for mankind, while **Michael Collins** orbited alone above.
In **1970**, an oxygen tank explosion crippled Apollo 13 on the way to the Moon, but the crew made it home safely.
On **July 17, 1975**, American and Soviet spacecraft **docked in orbit** and their crews shook hands, ending the Space Race.

new_recurring.rule: An old shortwave radio built from parts that belonged to Eli's grandfather. It wakes on its own whenever Eli is deep in a hands-on project late at night, locking onto a real moment from history and pulling him into it. A dry, calm voice…

story.title: Mia and the Ball That Keeps Score
story.subtitle: A journey through 2,000 years of kickoffs, rulebooks, and one very good dog

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Kickoff (2,000-ish Years Ago)
chapters.text:
Mia sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor at 11:40 p.m., laptop balanced on her knees, staring at a spreadsheet she'd built herself: shots, shots on target, conversion percentage. Column F was ugly. She'd missed a penalty that afternoon, and now she was doing what she always did with a bad stat — hunting for the pattern that explained it.

On the shelf above her desk sat Patches, a scuffed leather soccer ball with hand-stitched panels, a hand-me-down from her grandfather, who'd kicked it around a dirt lot as a kid. She glanced at it the way she always did before bed. Tonight the stitching was glowing.

"Don't look so surprised," said a voice that sounded like a radio announcer with a head cold. "You've had a rough match. Thought you could use a change of scene."

Mia blinked at the ball. "You're talking."

"I'm Patches. I keep stats older than your spreadsheet." The glow spread, the room folded like a map, and — **WHOOOSH** — Mia was standing in an open field under a sky that wasn't hers, next to a crowd of kids kicking a leather ball at two bamboo poles stuck in the dirt.

"Welcome to **China, over 2,000 years ago**," Patches said. "This game's called **cuju** — literally 'kick ball.' It's one of the oldest kicking games we've got records of, and a lot of people call it soccer's earliest known ancestor."

Mia counted heads on each side of the poles without meaning to — old habit. "That's not fair. Six against four."

"Sharp eyes," Patches said. "Tell them."

She jogged over and, with the kind of hand gestures that work in any century, moved two players across. The game evened out, speeding up, the ball snapping between feet. A kid on the smaller team punched the air as it threaded the poles.

"Guess uneven teams are a universal problem," Mia said.

"So is a good through ball," said Patches. "Nice fix. Kickoff."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Ball in the Wall (1314 and the 1540s)
chapters.text:
Mia barely had her footing before the ground thundered. A mob of men barreled past her — kicking, shoving, wrestling — a ball somewhere in the middle of forty bodies, rolling toward what used to be a vegetable stall.

"This," Patches said, "is called **mob football**. No ref, no field markings, sometimes the 'goal' is a church three miles away. It gets so out of hand that **King Edward II bans it in London in 1314** — his letter basically says 'too much noise, stop it.'"

Mia watched a cabbage cart get flattened and didn't need much convincing. "Yeah, I can see why."

"History's full of people discovering rules exist for a reason," said Patches, and the scene dissolved into stone corridors — cold, echoing, a castle instead of a street. "**Stirling Castle**, Scotland. Different century. Somewhere in these walls is a find that'll make your stats brain happy."

Mia ran a hand along the wood paneling the way she scanned a stat sheet for the one number that didn't belong. One panel sat a few inches proud of the rest. "This one's off."

She pressed it. It popped open, and inside sat a small, lumpy, ancient-looking ball, stitched from hand-cut leather.

"Found behind paneling just like that, for real," Patches said. "Experts think it might go back to the **1540s**, which would make it the oldest football in the world."

"It's smaller than I expected."

"It's a **pig's bladder** wrapped in leather. Don't think about it too hard."

Mia didn't. "A five-hundred-year-old ball just chilling behind a wall. That's a stat nobody saw coming."

"Welcome to history," Patches said. "It's mostly stuff that got left behind on purpose, and then found by accident."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Writing It Down (1848–1863)
chapters.text:
Next stop dropped Mia into a wood-paneled room crowded with university students arguing loudly over a sheet of paper, pencils passed around like contraband.

"**Cambridge, 1848**," Patches said. "Different schools play different versions of football. Some let you carry the ball. Some don't. Nobody can agree how many players make a team, either."

"How is anyone supposed to keep stats on that?" Mia said, mostly to herself. "If every school plays different rules, you can't even compare one match to another."

One student overheard her and went still, like she'd said something useful. He grabbed a fresh sheet and wrote **"Cambridge Rules"** across the top.

"Nice nudge," Patches said, as the room dissolved. "It's an early try at one shared rulebook. Doesn't fully stick yet, but it gets the idea moving."

They landed next in a London meeting room, 1863, where a man with excellent sideburns was hunched over a notebook, ink-stained fingers flying. "**Ebenezer Cobb Morley**," Patches said. "On **October 26, 1863**, he and a room full of club reps start something called the **Football Association** — the FA. Morley personally writes the first official rulebook, the Laws of the Game."

Mia leaned over his shoulder and watched him underline one sentence twice: no carrying the ball with your hands.

"That's the rule that actually splits soccer from rugby," Patches said. "Before this, some clubs allowed it. After this, if you want to play this version, hands are out."

"And the name?" Mia asked. "Why's it called soccer in some places and football everywhere else?"

"English schoolboys in the **1880s** started calling 'association football' '**assoc**' for short," said Patches. "Say that fast enough times and you get 'soccer.' Both names describe the exact same game. People have been arguing over which one's correct for a century and a half."

Mia grinned. "Statistically, neither of them wins."

"Full time," Patches said. "For this stop, anyway."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Firsts (1871–1888)
chapters.text:
Patches dropped Mia onto the edge of a packed pitch in **Glasgow, 1872**, under a sky the color of wet concrete. Thousands of spectators stood shoulder to shoulder behind a rope.

"This is the **first official international match ever played** — **Scotland versus England**," Patches said. "Before this, teams only played other clubs in their own country."

Mia watched ninety minutes of hard-fought, bone-rattling soccer that ended exactly the way the scoreboard started.

"Wait," she said. "**0–0**? That's the whole match?"

"That's the whole match," Patches confirmed. "First international fixture in history, and it's a scoreless draw. Somewhere, a stats nerd from the future is very disappointed in both teams."

"I'm right here," Mia said. "And honestly? Respect to the defenses."

They jumped sideways to a knockout tournament already underway — the **FA Cup**, first played in **1871–72**, which Patches noted was still running every single year since, making it the oldest football competition still going anywhere in the world.

Then the scene shifted again, this time to a crowded meeting room, **1888**, where a stocky man with a notebook was arguing with a table of club owners.

"**William McGregor**," Patches said. "He wants to turn a pile of one-off club matches into something organized. Problem is, nobody can agree how to decide who's actually the best team over a whole season."

Mia thought about her own spreadsheet — wins, losses, draws, tallied up, totaled into something you could actually rank. "Just... give points for each result. A win's worth more than a draw. Add it all up at the end. Whoever's got the most points is best."

McGregor stopped mid-argument and stared at her like she'd solved something. He started writing.

"And that," Patches said, "is basically the league table that every soccer competition on Earth still uses. McGregor founds the **Football League** that same year — the first one in the world."

"I didn't invent the points table," Mia said.

"No," Patches agreed. "But you'd have fit right in with the people who did."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Going Global (1904–1930)
chapters.text:
The next stop smelled like coffee and old paper. **Paris, 1904.** Seven men sat around a table covered in documents, looking like they were about to sign something important, mostly because they were.

Mia scanned the parchment upside down, the way she scanned any list of numbers. "Seven countries?"

"**Seven**," Patches confirmed. "They're founding **FIFA** — football's first world governing body — right here, right now."

"That's it? Seven signatures and now there's a whole planet's worth of soccer?"

"Rome wasn't built in a day. Neither was the World Cup. That takes another **twenty-six years**."

The scene shifted to a brand-new stadium, flags snapping in warm wind, a trophy gleaming on a velvet cushion nearby. "**Uruguay, 1930**," Patches said. "First-ever **FIFA World Cup**. Host country's in the final."

Mia leaned close to the trophy, reading tiny engraved letters along its base. "Is this named after a person?"

"Go on, guess."

She thought about who'd want a trophy named after them for driving the whole thing into existence. "The guy who actually made this happen?"

"**Jules Rimet**," Patches said. "FIFA's president. He's the one who pushes hardest to make a World Cup real, so the first trophy carries his name."

On the pitch, the host team lifted the ball over their heads, having beaten **Argentina** in the final.

"Uruguay wins the first one," Patches said. "Home advantage, apparently, works on more than just travel costs."

"I'd need the full shot chart to really judge that," Mia said.

"Of course you would. You'd have had a spreadsheet open before kickoff."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Three Golden Cups (1958–1970)
chapters.text:
Patches skipped them forward into a roaring stadium, yellow-and-green jerseys streaming across the grass. "Quick quiz," Patches said. "How many World Cups has one country won, all-time record?"

"Give me the years and I'll tell you who," Mia said.

"**1958. 1962. 1970. 1994. 2002.**"

"That's five. Nobody else is close. Has to be **Brazil**."

"Correct. Still the record today." The crowd roared louder as a slim, grinning forward curled a shot into the net. "And that's **Pelé** — the only player in history on **three** of those winning squads: **1958, 1962, and 1970**."

Mia watched him glide past two defenders like they were cones in a drill. "Three World Cups. That's not a stat, that's a cheat code."

They jumped to a different 1970 match, a referee jogging across the pitch holding up a small colored card. Mia frowned. "Why's he doing that?"

"Guess," said Patches.

She clocked the referee's route, past a set of traffic lights outside the stadium gates, red on top, yellow below. "The colors. Is it like a traffic signal? Yellow means slow down, red means you're out?"

"Exactly that," Patches said. "Referee **Ken Aston** gets the idea from a traffic light on his drive home, after a match where nobody could tell if a player had actually been sent off. **Yellow and red cards debut at the 1970 World Cup** and they've been standard ever since."

"So soccer's discipline system is just traffic rules for humans."

"Most good ideas are stolen from somewhere boring," Patches said. "Welcome to officiating."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Dog Who Found the Cup (1966–1974)
chapters.text:
London again, but a different, grayer year. A newspaper stand had a headline so big Mia could read it from across the street: WORLD CUP STOLEN.

"**1966**," Patches said. "The actual trophy, on public display before the tournament, gets stolen right out from under everyone's noses."

Mia narrowed her eyes at the chaos of police and reporters. "Do they get it back?"

"Give it a week."

She thought it through like a detective working a box score. "Somebody who wasn't even looking for a trophy. Somebody low to the ground. Somebody who sniffs stuff for a living."

Patches made a sound like a laugh with static in it. "You're closer than you think."

A week later — the scene jumped forward, same street — a small dog nosed at a garden hedge and came up with a package wrapped in newspaper. Inside: the trophy, completely unharmed.

"A **dog named Pickles** finds it, wrapped up under a hedge," Patches said. "National hero. Gets his photo in actual newspapers."

"I called the sniffing part," Mia said. "I'm taking credit for that."

England went on to host and win that tournament — "**their only World Cup title so far**," Patches noted — and then the scene slid forward again, into a different decade. A new, smaller trophy sat in a glass case, replacing the old one.

"Why's this one different?" Mia asked.

"Brazil's third win, back in 1970, came with a prize," Patches said. "Win it three times, you keep the original trophy forever. So in **1974**, FIFA had to make a brand-new one for everybody else to fight over."

"They basically out-statted the entire sport into retiring a trophy."

"That's one way to put it."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Fifty Years Benched (1921–1991)
chapters.text:
The next stop was a packed stadium, tens of thousands of fans on their feet, cheering a team in matching shirts and skirts running the ball down the wing. A player with a ferocious shot curled one into the net from an angle Mia wouldn't have even attempted.

"**Lily Parr**," Patches said. "Star player for the **Dick, Kerr Ladies**, one of the most popular teams in England. Full stop — men's or women's."

"Then why haven't I heard of her?"

Patches didn't answer right away, and the scene changed — the same stadium, no crowd, gates padlocked, a faded notice pinned to the fence. Mia read it twice to make sure she wasn't misreading it.

"**1921**," Patches said quietly. "The FA bans women's football from its grounds. Says it's 'unsuitable.' No real reason given that holds up."

Mia's jaw tightened. "That's not fair."

"It wasn't."

She did the math before Patches could say it, the way she always reached for the number first. "When does it actually get lifted?"

"**1971**."

"That's—" she stopped, recalculating to be sure. "That's **fifty years**. Fifty years of a team that good, benched, for nothing."

"Fifty years," Patches agreed. "But it doesn't end there."

The scene shifted one last time: a stadium in **China, 1991**, a trophy lifted by a team in white and blue. "First-ever official **Women's World Cup**," Patches said. "**The United States** wins it."

Mia watched the celebration, still doing the math in her head — the gap, the comeback, the two numbers that told the whole story better than any paragraph could.

"Fifty years missing from the record book," she said, "and then right back to winning it."

"That's the stat worth remembering," Patches said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Full Time
chapters.text:
The glow folded back in on itself, and Mia landed, cross-legged, exactly where she'd started — laptop open, spreadsheet glowing on the screen, Patches sitting quiet and scuffed on the shelf like nothing had happened.

Except Column F didn't look so ugly anymore. One missed penalty, one afternoon, in a game that people had spent **over two thousand years** arguing rules into shape, writing down, banning, unbanning, and fighting to be allowed to play at all.

"You good?" Patches asked, voice back to its usual crackle.

Mia looked at her spreadsheet, then back at the ball. "You know how many World Cups Brazil's won?"

"Five. You told me that one, actually."

"Right." She smiled, closed the laptop, and set it by her bed. "I've got training Thursday. I'm going to try that penalty again."

"Kickoff," Patches said, which from an old leather ball was apparently also how you said goodnight.

Mia turned off the lamp and lay back, running the numbers one more time, already half-planning the run-up.

story.ending_line: Thursday couldn't come soon enough.

true_facts.text: **Cuju**, a ball-kicking game played in China over **2,000 years ago**, is one of soccer's earliest known ancestors.
Mob football was so chaotic that **King Edward II banned it in London in 1314**.
A leather ball found hidden behind paneling at **Stirling Castle** may date to the **1540s**, possibly the oldest football in the world.
The **Football Association** was founded in London on **October 26, 1863**, and banned carrying the ball with your hands.
**Ebenezer Cobb Morley** personally wrote the first official rulebook, the Laws of the Game, in 1863.
The **first-ever international match**, Scotland versus England, ended **0-0** in 1872.
**William McGregor** organized the **Football League** in 1888 — the first organized league in the world.
**FIFA** was founded in Paris in 1904 by just **seven countries**.
The **first World Cup** was held in **Uruguay in 1930**, and the host beat Argentina in the final.
**Brazil** holds the all-time World Cup record with **five titles**: 1958, 1962, 1970, 1994, and 2002.
**Yellow and red cards**, invented by referee Ken Aston after he got the idea from a traffic light, first appeared at the **1970 World Cup**.
The World Cup trophy was **stolen in 1966** and found a week later by a **dog named Pickles**.
The FA's ban on women's football was finally lifted in **1971**, **fifty years** after it began.

new_recurring.name: Patches
new_recurring.rule: A scuffed, hand-stitched leather soccer ball on the child's shelf, glows along its seams to start a journey through sports history. Speaks like a dry, crackly radio announcer. Always says 'Kickoff' to start a trip and 'Full time' to close…

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Mia lands back on her bedroom floor exactly where she started, her stat spreadsheet still open but no longer bothering her, Patches quiet on the shelf, and she turns off the lamp already planning to retry her missed penalty at Thursday's training.

story.title: Noah and the Ninety-Minute Loop
story.subtitle: A gamer's guide to why the body needs a save point

chapters.heading: New Save File: Chicago, 1953
chapters.text:
Noah was flat on his bedroom floor at 2:47 a.m., phone propped on a tower of game cases, one earbud in, thumb scrolling a highlight reel he'd already watched twice. A half-finished beat looped in his other ear — the kind of three-chord loop that sounds genius at 3 a.m. and embarrassing by noon.

The screen glitched: black, then a sick phosphor green, like a monitor from before he was born. A forgotten app icon — a pixel crescent moon wearing tiny headphones — pulsed in the corner. He tapped it, which is how most disasters start.

"You've been awake nineteen hours and forty minutes," said the icon, now standing on his nightstand as a glowing block the size of a soda can. "I'm Circa. Want to know why that counts?"

Noah had slept through worse jump scares. "Sure."

Green light swallowed the room. When it cleared, he stood in a cramped lab that smelled like old wiring, watching a sleeping boy wired near the eyes.

"Chicago, **1953**," Circa said. "That's **Eugene Aserinsky**. He's about to notice something nobody's written down yet."

Under the boy's eyelids, his eyes flicked fast, side to side — exactly like the idle-twitch his rhythm game gave a paused character so you'd know it wasn't frozen.

"That's not frozen," Noah said. "His brain's doing something."

"Bingo. Aserinsky and his professor, **Nathaniel Kleitman**, called it **REM — rapid eye movement sleep**. First proof the sleeping brain never actually shuts off."

"So I've been staring at loading screens my whole life and missed that the game was still running."

"Close enough. Six more levels. Earbud in."

chapters.heading: Level 2: The 90-Minute Loop
chapters.text:
The lab dissolved into a looping green progress bar, spinning like a console booting up. "Every night," Circa said, "you cycle through stages about every **ninety minutes** — quiet sleep, then active, dream-heavy **REM**, back and forth, again and again."

Noah did the math out loud. "That's basically two full albums back to back."

"Test it tomorrow night. See how far you get."

The bar split to show a second sleeper, limbs loose, face slack, eyes still flicking underneath. "During REM," Circa said, "the brain's almost as busy as when you're awake. But your muscles go limp — your body hits mute so you can't act out whatever you're dreaming."

Noah frowned. "Then why do people sleepwalk? Saw it happen at camp. Kid wandered into the kitchen."

"Different stage. Sleepwalking happens during deep, quiet non-REM sleep, not during dreaming. He wasn't acting anything out — his body was just up before his brain was."

"So the camp kid wasn't fighting imaginary zombies."

"Statistically unlikely. Though I can't rule it out for that one kid specifically."

Noah laughed, which echoed strangely in the glowing void. He noticed the pattern now — on, off, on, off, like a controller vibrating through a cutscene where you can't move, but something's definitely happening on screen.

"Okay," he said. "I get it. Sleep isn't a pause menu."

"Now you're playing the right game," said Circa.

chapters.heading: Boss Fight: The Growth Stat
chapters.text:
The next room looked like his own, except the guitar in the corner was his — the one he'd been grinding a riff on for a week without nailing it.

"The deepest stage of non-REM sleep," Circa said, "is when your body releases the most growth hormone — one reason a growing body like yours needs more sleep than mine."

"You don't have a body."

"Exactly why I never grow. Focus."

Circa pulled up a second screen: Noah, three nights ago, replaying his own practice clips at 1 a.m. instead of sleeping, trying to memorize the riff through pure repetition.

"Sleep also sorts your day into long-term memory," Circa said. "What you practice, then actually sleep on, sticks better than extra reps at 1 a.m."

Noah winced. "So all those late-night re-watches—"

"Were probably worse than just going to bed."

He picked up the guitar, played the riff clean on the first try, and stared at his own fingers like they'd betrayed him. "That's annoying."

"That's biology."

"Fine. I'll test it. Sleep tonight, riff tomorrow."

"That's the whole point of this level."

chapters.heading: Debug Mode: The Master Clock
chapters.text:
The room shifted again, this time into something like the inside of a skull rendered in wireframe — a small structure glowing right behind the eyes.

"This is the **suprachiasmatic nucleus**," Circa said. "A tiny cluster of brain cells, sitting right where your eye nerves cross. It's your body's master clock — it decides when you feel sleepy and when you feel awake."

"That's a lot of syllables for an alarm clock."

"The clock itself has a name too: **circadian**. From Latin — *circa* meaning 'about,' *diem* meaning 'a day.' About a day. That's the whole rhythm."

Noah blinked. "Circa. Like — you."

"I was wondering when you'd notice."

"You named yourself after a vocabulary word."

"I named myself after the most important clock in your body. You're welcome. And it's also why staring at a bright phone at 3 a.m. confuses it — light tells the clock it's still daytime, even when it very much isn't."

Noah grinned despite himself. "Okay, that's actually a decent bit."

"I've had a while to write it."

chapters.heading: Achievement Unlocked: The Clock Genes
chapters.text:
Circa opened a window, cutscene-sized, showing a single unimpressed fruit fly drifting in midair.

"In **2017**, three scientists — **Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash, and Michael Young** — won the **Nobel Prize** for finding the actual genes that keep a circadian clock ticking."

"They won a Nobel Prize for bugs?"

"They won it for using fruit flies to find the genes, because even fruit flies show sleep-like rest. Turns out the genes work almost the same way in you."

Noah studied the fly, unimpressed back. "So this thing's running basically the same software I am."

"A much older build. Sleep showed up in something this small a very long time ago — long before there were screens, songs, or speedrunners to lose sleep over."

"Respect," Noah told the fly.

It ignored him completely.

"It's asleep," Circa said. "It was always going to ignore you."

Noah decided that was either the most humbling or most reassuring thing he'd heard all night — possibly both. If even a fly needed downtime, maybe his 3 a.m. mixing sessions could wait until after an actual night's sleep.

chapters.heading: Side Quest: The Dimmer Switch
chapters.text:
Circa led him into a hallway lined with the exact lamp from Noah's room, dimmed low. "In **1958**, a scientist named **Aaron Lerner** and his team isolated **melatonin** — the sleepy-time hormone — for the first time."

"Isolated how?"

"From glands in animals, in a lab. Point is, your body makes its own, and bright light — like, say, a phone screen at 3 a.m. — tells your brain to make less of it."

Noah glanced at his own phone, screen still blazing white in his pocket. "That's — unfortunately relevant."

"Dim it. See what happens."

He thumbed the brightness down. The hallway lamp dimmed in sync, and something in his chest actually loosened, like a level finally saving.

"There's also a cleanup crew," Circa added. "While you sleep, your brain runs something like a nightly rinse cycle, flushing out waste that builds up during the day."

"Like defragging a hard drive."

"If your hard drive also repaired itself and took out the trash, sure."

Noah pocketed the dim phone. "So skipping sleep is basically running on a full hard drive with the fan unplugged."

"That's the most accurate metaphor anyone's used in this room all night."

chapters.heading: Challenge Mode: The Eleven-Day Run
chapters.text:
Circa flashed a new window: a teenager propped in front of a pinball machine at 3 a.m., eyes wide open on sheer willpower.

"San Diego, **1964**," Circa said. "**Randy Gardner**, seventeen years old, stayed awake for about **eleven days** straight, for a science-fair project. One of the longest stretches anyone's ever gone without sleep — and people still talk about it."

Noah's gamer brain lit up instantly. "Eleven days. That's basically a world record. I could probably—"

"Don't," Circa cut in, sharp enough that the green light flickered. "Doctors don't recommend anyone try to beat it. Go without sleep that long and your mood, your focus, your memory — basically every stat you actually care about — tanks fast."

Noah studied the kid on the glowing screen: grinning, glassy-eyed, clearly running on fumes instead of sleep. He thought of every night he'd stayed up remixing one chorus, convinced just one more pass would fix it. Eleven days sounded like the least efficient grind he'd ever heard of.

"So he's not the hero of this level."

"He's the warning label," Circa said. "Great story. Terrible plan. Nobody's supposed to try to beat that number."

Noah pulled his phone from his pocket, screen still glowing faintly through the fabric, and powered it all the way off instead of just dimming it.

"Yeah, I'm good. I'd like to remember my own name tomorrow."

"That," Circa said, almost sounding relieved for a glowing rectangle, "might be the smartest move you've made all night."

chapters.heading: Final Level: Logging Off
chapters.text:
The hallway folded into a wide screen: ocean, then grassland, then a dim cave, flicking like channels on an old TV.

"Before you log off," Circa said, "a few side characters." A bottlenose dolphin drifted past, one eye open, half its brain clearly dark and resting. "Dolphins and some seals sleep with half their brain at a time. One eye stays open, watching for danger, or keeping them swimming."

"So they never fully go offline."

"Never fully. Unlike this one." The scene cut to a giraffe folding its long legs into an awkward nap. "Giraffes are some of the shortest sleepers of any big animal — sometimes under **two hours a day**, grabbed in short naps standing up."

"Two hours? And I complain about eight."

"Then there's this guy." A small bat hung upside down, perfectly still. "Some bats sleep up to **twenty hours a day**. Biggest couch potato in the animal kingdom, no contest."

Noah laughed. "Put that on a shirt."

Circa pulled up one more window: a yellowed old book cover. "Back in **1899**, a guy named **Sigmund Freud** wrote a whole book arguing dreams reveal your secret hidden wishes. Most scientists today don't buy the specifics, honestly. But it's part of why people started taking dreams seriously enough to study, instead of just shrugging them off."

"Guess even a rough draft counts for something," Noah said.

"Add it all up over a lifetime," Circa said, "and you'll spend roughly **a third of your life** asleep. Not wasted time. Maintenance time. Kleitman — the professor from your very first level — spent his whole career proving that. People still call him the father of modern sleep research."

The green light folded in on itself, and Noah dropped back onto his bedroom floor exactly where he'd started: phone dark on the carpet, one earbud dangling, the half-finished beat silent for once.

Circa shrank back down into a pixel crescent moon in the corner of the screen, tiny headphones and all. "Same time tomorrow?"

"Depends," Noah said, already reaching to plug the phone in and do absolutely nothing else with it. "You got more levels?"

"Always. Go recharge the actual hardware first."

He pulled a blanket off the floor, left the screen dim, and let the loop finally rest.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, he had a riff to finally nail — rested, for once.

true_facts.text: In **1953**, **Eugene Aserinsky** noticed a sleeping boy's eyes flicking fast under his eyelids, and he and **Nathaniel Kleitman** named it **REM sleep**.
A night's sleep moves in repeating cycles about **ninety minutes** long, switching between quiet sleep and active REM sleep.
During REM sleep the brain is almost as busy as when you're awake, but your muscles go limp so you can't act out your dreams.
Sleepwalking happens during deep, quiet non-REM sleep, not during dreaming — so sleepwalkers usually aren't acting out a dream.
The deepest stage of non-REM sleep triggers the most growth hormone, which is one reason a growing body needs extra sleep.
Sleep helps the brain sort the day's experiences into long-term memory, so sleeping on something you practiced helps it stick.
A tiny cluster of brain cells called the **suprachiasmatic nucleus**, sitting right where your eye nerves cross, works as the body's master clock.
The word **circadian** comes from Latin words meaning "about a day" — which is roughly how long the body's clock runs.
In **2017**, three scientists — **Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash, and Michael Young** — won the **Nobel Prize** for finding the genes that keep that clock ticking.
Even fruit flies show sleep-like rest, which means sleep has probably been around in living things for a very long time.
In **1958**, scientist **Aaron Lerner** and his team first isolated **melatonin**, the hormone that makes you feel sleepy.
In **1964**, seventeen-year-old **Randy Gardner** stayed awake for about **eleven days** for a science project — one of the longest stretches ever recorded.
Doctors say nobody should try to repeat that — going without sleep wrecks your mood, focus, and memory fast.
Back in **1899**, **Sigmund Freud** wrote a famous book claiming dreams reveal secret wishes — most scientists today don't buy the specifics, but it got people studying dreams seriously.
